title: King Charles draws ‘line in the sand’ with Prince Harry, Meghan Markle after couple caught off guard: expert
summary: King Charles drew a firm line with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle in a letter clarifying their royal status, but Uganda's Invictus Games exit added fuel.
story: King Charles confirms Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will not return to royal duties. A letter sent on behalf of the King explains their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and they are now akin to private citizens.
King Charles III has drawn a firm "line in the sand" with Prince Harry and Meghan Markle after sending a letter spelling out their royal standing.

The claim was made by British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard after the Duke and Duchess of Sussex told People magazine they were "surprised" by the timing of a letter circulated by Buckingham Palace clarifying their non-working royal status.

"King Charles' narrative is decisive as he draws a line in the sand — nothing new here, no more discussion required," Chard told Fox News Digital. "I'm sure the Sussexes expected flexibility. Prince Harry may be the king's son, but he lacks power to amend and dictate the monarch's statement."
KING CHARLES III CLARIFIES PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE WILL NOT RESUME ROYAL DUTIES AFTER UK MOVE

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex leave St. Paul's Cathedral after attending the Service of Thanksgiving during Queen Elizabeth II's Platinum Jubilee celebrations in London in 2022. (Wiktor Szymanowicz/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

On Sept. 7, a senior palace official reiterated that Harry and Meghan are non-working royals, according to People magazine. The letter, which was issued on behalf of the king, was said to have been shared with the Sussexes. A spokesperson for the couple said they were "a little surprised not to have been told about this in advance," the BBC reported.

Those close to the couple told People magazine they received the letter and, 20 minutes later, sent back some questions. However, they were told that the letter had already been circulated to the media.
The former Prince Charles, with Prince Harry and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex during Trooping the Colour on June 9, 2018, in London. (UK Press via Getty Images)

The letter issued by the Lord Chamberlain, Richard Benyon, Lord Benyon, at the king's direction, pointed out that the couple were "private citizens" and their His and Her Royal Highness styles remain in abeyance and are not used.
WATCH: KING CHARLES CONFIRMS PRINCE HARRY AND MEGHAN MARKLE WILL NOT RETURN TO ROYAL DUTIES
Chard told Fox News Digital the guidance made one thing clear: they "do not represent the Crown."

"There is no ambiguity about who is in and who is out," she said. "The king is protecting the institution. The public has made it clear they do not want the monarchy to be undermined or damaged by confusion. The letter's statement puts minds at rest."

Prince Harry leaves the High Court in central London on April 8, 2025, after a hearing on the British government's decision to downgrade his personal security during visits to Britain. (Justin Tallis/AFP via Getty Images)

"In part, yes, the monarchy can only have one voice," Chard shared. "Prince William and Princess Catherine are the future king and queen. They officially speak for the crown alongside King Charles and Queen Camilla. It's constitutional, and the crown takes precedence."
Prince William, Prince of Wales, seen here with Catherine, Princess of Wales, is heir to the British throne. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)
Royal commentator Richard Fitzwilliams said there's another, more silent message the king wants to convey.
"The letter states the palace’s position, but it’s clearly intended as a put-down after the way the royals were blindsided by the Sussexes returning to Britain," he claimed.
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle relocated to California in 2020. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"The Sussexes see themselves as public figures, not private citizens," he said. "So, they are ‘surprised,’ but are unlikely to alter their plans. The king was never going to debate anything with the Sussexes. The royals don’t debate, although Queen Elizabeth’s ‘recollections may vary’ is legendary."
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Queen Elizabeth II, Meghan Markle and Prince Harry watch a flypast to mark the centenary of the Royal Air Force from the balcony of Buckingham Palace on July 10, 2018, in London. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)
The couple relocated to Britain in August ahead of their children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, starting school.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of The Sovereign, and are no longer working Members of The Royal Family," stated the letter, as quoted by People. "This position, distinct from the State and Royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected."
Queen Elizabeth II during the wedding of Prince Harry to Meghan Markle on May 19, 2018, in Windsor, England. (Jonathan Brady - WPA Pool/Getty Images)

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex," it continued. "Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used. The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."
Prince Harry departs from The Invictus Games Foundation Conversation: From Policy to Practice at Chatham House on July 7, 2026, in London. (Eamonn M. McCormack/Getty Images)
Chard called it a "reality check" for the Sussexes.

"It shouldn’t have been a shock," she said. "The update was inevitable and warranted. Harry and Meghan unexpectedly swanned back to the U.K. and seemingly hoped to continue as if they were still working royals. The blurred lines created an air of confusion, with the majority wondering if Harry was back in the fold of the institution. The petty comment batted back from Team Sussex highlighted bruised egos."
Prince Harry's book "Spare" is displayed in a bookstore on Dec. 16, 2023, in Bath, England. (Matt Cardy/Getty Images)

"Allegedly the Sussexes were caught off guard. The irony when you consider Harry’s book ‘Spare,’ their Netflix documentaries and the Oprah interview catching the British royal family off guard over the years."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Meghan Markle is seen here being interviewed by Oprah Winfrey on March 8, 2021. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

According to People, Harry is preparing to kick off a series of charitable engagements that were planned well ahead of the couple’s return to the U.K. These events will highlight charities and causes he supports, including the Invictus Games. The next iteration of the sporting competition is taking place in 2027 in Birmingham, England.
However, Harry is already facing a rocky arrival.
Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, Uganda's chief of defense forces and eldest son of President Yoweri Museveni, on May 13, 2025, in Kampala, Uganda. (Getty Images)
On Sept. 9, Gen. Muhoozi Kainerugaba, the son of Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni and head of the country's armed forces, announced that his country was withdrawing from the Invictus Games.
Prince Charles and Prince Harry attend the "Our Planet" global premiere at the Natural History Museum in London on April 4, 2019. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," he wrote on X. "We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."
Gen. Kainerugaba also told The Times of London, "I have factions in the Ministry of Defence that support that Harry-Meghan nonsense. I had to quash it straight away. I support the monarch. Period."

The Duke of Sussex arrives for an Invictus Games Foundation meeting July 7, 2026, part of the One Year to Go celebrations for the Invictus Games Birmingham 2027. (Stefan Rousseau/PA Images via Getty Images)

A source close to Harry went on to tell People, "They made it very clear that the reason they pulled out was a direct result of perceived guidance from the Lord Chamberlain. This was an unintended or intended consequence of the letter — and that was always going to happen. Hence the wish not to rush it out."
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
Prince Harry waves as he departs after a visit to the Centre for Blast Injury Studies at Imperial College London on Sept. 10, 2025. (Getty Images)
"The only people suffering as a result are the competitors from Uganda who would have been taking part in next year’s Invictus Games," the insider added.
British royal expert Hilary Fordwich wasn't buying it.

Meghan, Duchess of Sussex attends an Invictus Games Friends and Family reception hosted by the City of The Hague and the Dutch Ministry of Defense at Zuiderpark on April 15, 2022, in The Hague, Netherlands. (Max Mumby/Indigo/Getty Images)

"Harry blaming this letter for Uganda pulling out of the Invictus Games is a ghastly move on his part," she said. "No doubt Harry and Meghan thought King Charles would accommodate their return or at least consult with them. But their expectations weren't relevant for the royals."

Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex, and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, attend the David Foster Foundation 40th Anniversary Celebration on Aug. 7, 2026, in Victoria, British Columbia. (The David Foster Foundation via Getty Images)
Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner told Fox News Digital he believes the letter has caused more harm than good in any peace talks Harry is willing to have with his estranged family.

"My personal opinion on the decision by King Charles to make public a letter conceived by the Lord Chamberlain to reiterate that Harry and Meghan were not working royals was an act of malicious intent initiated by those intending to disrupt their return," he explained.

King Charles III is crowned with St. Edward's Crown by the Archbishop of Canterbury, the Most Rev. Justin Welby, during his coronation ceremony at Westminster Abbey in London, England, on May 6, 2023. (Getty Images)
"The message was unjustified," said Turner. "I hope Harry and Meghan will not rise to the bait and retaliate but calmly move on."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Meghan Markle and Prince Harry attend the wheelchair basketball event during Day 1 of the Invictus Games at the Vancouver Convention Centre in British Columbia, on Feb. 9, 2025. (Karwai Tang/WireImage)

People reported that the king remains supportive of organizations and initiatives, like the Invictus Games, that help wounded service personnel. Palace insiders also pointed out that the letter does not represent a new policy but instead reiterates the terms agreed to at the 2020 "Sandringham Summit" led by the late queen. The family meeting took place shortly before Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior working royals and moved to California.
Royal author Robert Jobson previously told The Daily Mail that "there won't be any war of words" between the king and his younger son.
King Charles, Queen Camilla and Meghan, Duchess of Sussex are seen here in Buckingham Palace in London, on May 22, 2018. (Chris Jackson/Getty Images)

"Perhaps predictably, there was an immediate response from the couple," he told the outlet. "But don’t expect to see anything similar coming from the palace. The king has no intention of being drawn into responding further."
King Charles III and Prince William attend the Thistle Service at St Giles' Cathedral in Edinburgh, Scotland, on July 1, 2026. (Getty Images)

While the Sussexes have returned to the U.K. for an extended stay, they won't resume their roles as working royals. They will live in a private, nonroyal residence outside London while maintaining their California home and a property in Portugal.
Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Celine Dion breaks down onstage during emotional return after 6-year hiatus
summary: Celine Dion opened her 26-show Paris residency with tears of joy and a powerful promise fulfilled after six years battling stiff person syndrome.
story: Amy Grant recalls how a chance doctor visit saved her life. The singer was diagnosed with a potentially catastrophic heart condition after  accompanying husband Vince Gill to his cardiologist appointment.
Celine Dion made her return to the stage for the first time in six years while continuing her battle with stiff-person syndrome, and the occasion proved every bit as emotional as anticipated.

The 58-year-old singer — who launched her 26-show residency at the Plenitude Arena in Paris, France, on Sept. 12 - opened the concert with her French-language song "On Ne Change Pas" before tearing up, according to multiple videos circulating online.
"These are, of course, tears of joy. I’m so delighted to see you," Dion told the crowd, according to People.
CELINE DION REVEALS INCURABLE NEUROLOGICAL DISORDER DIAGNOSIS IN EMOTIONAL VIDEO
Celine Dion performs on the opening night of her residency at Paris La Defense Arena on Sept. 12, 2026, in Nanterre, France. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Dion later addressed the significance of the performance and her long-awaited return.
"I made a promise to come back, to be back on stage," she said. "So here I am, singing for you and singing for me, singing life!"
BILLY RAY CYRUS CHEATED DEATH DURING SEPSIS, VOCAL PARALYSIS BATTLE BEFORE STAGING MUSIC COMEBACK

The singer also thanked fans for their support and patience during her years away from the stage, telling them, "I am everything I am because you loved me," before performing her hit "Because You Loved Me."

Dion’s career was first interrupted in 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic forced her to postpone the "Courage World Tour." In January 2022, she canceled the North American leg of the tour, explaining that her recovery from severe muscle spasms was taking longer than expected.

Dion became emotional just minutes into her set. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
BARRY MANILOW, 82, GIVES UPDATE ON HIS CANCER BATTLE AS HE CANCELS MORE TOUR DATES
At the time, Dion said she was following the treatment regimen prescribed by her doctors and hoped to return to performing once she regained her health.
Months later, Dion revealed the diagnosis behind her health struggles in an emotional video shared with fans.

"As you know, I've always been an open book. And I wasn't ready to say anything before — but I'm ready now. I've been dealing with problems with my health for a long time. And it's been really difficult for me to face these challenges and talk about everything that I've been going through."
Dion then revealed she had been diagnosed with Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS), which she explained "affects something like one in a million people."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

SPS is defined by the Cleveland Clinic as "a rare autoimmune movement disorder that affects the central nervous system (the brain and spinal cord). People with this condition first experience a stiffening of the muscles of their trunk followed, over time, by the development of stiffness and rigidity in the legs and other muscles in the body."
The Canadian singer revealed her stiff-person diagnosis in 2022. (AFP via Getty Images)
Dion explained that the condition sometimes made it difficult for her to walk and prevented her from using her vocal cords "to sing the way I’m used to."
JON BON JOVI ABRUPTLY ENDS MADISON SQUARE GARDEN SHOW AFTER HEALTH SETBACK
"All I know is singing," Dion said at the time. "It’s what I’ve done all my life. And it’s what I love to do the most."

Dion offered fans a glimpse of her progress in 2024. She received a standing ovation when she appeared at the Grammy Awards to present the album of the year and later documented her health journey in the Prime Video documentary "I Am: Celine Dion."

In July 2024, Dion performed Edith Piaf’s "L’Hymne à l’amour" at the Paris Olympics opening ceremony. The appearance marked her first live performance since revealing her diagnosis and was viewed as a hopeful sign that she could eventually return to concerts.
Celine Dion attends the "I Am: Celine Dion" special screening at Alice Tully Hall in New York City on June 17, 2024. (Getty Images)
Dion’s Paris residency is expected to feature some of her biggest hits, including "My Heart Will Go On," "It’s All Coming Back to Me Now" and "Because You Loved Me."
The singer previously said that touring could be difficult even when she was healthy, but she refused to give up on performing.

title: Dolph Lundgren and wife Emma Krokdal enjoy date night at Arnold Schwarzenegger’s charity event

story: Lundgren said "age is just a number" to him and that he doesnt care what people have to say about his relationship.
Dolph Lundgren was spotted stepping out for a date night in Beverly Hills, California with his wife Emma Krokdal.
The 68-year-old "Rocky" star was all smiles as he and Krokdal, 30, attended Arnold Schwarzenegger's All-Stars for Change charity event at Novikov Beverly Hills on Friday night.

Lundgren sported a black suit, a white dress shirt and gray sneakers while Krokdal wore a black one-shoulder chiffon top which she paired with a black asymmetrical satin wrap miniskirt, beige sequinned peep toe heels and a burnt orange satin clutch.
The couple, who tied the knot at their villa in Mykonos, Greece, in July 2023, beamed while posing for photos at the upscale Italian-Mediterranean restaurant.
Dolph Lundgren and his wife Emma Krokdal stepped out for a date night at Arnold Schwarzenegger's fundraiser. (Backgrid)
The fundraiser benefited After-School All-Stars, a national nonprofit providing free after-school and summer programs for youth that Schwarzenegger founded in 1992.
NOAH WYLE, MATT DAMON, LEONARDO DICAPRIO STILL CAPTIVATING AUDIENCES WELL INTO THEIR 50S

Lundgren also stepped behind the bar to mix cocktails for guests during the event, which was sponsored by his vodka brand, Hard Cut Vodka. Lundgren and Krokdal co-founded Hard Cut in 2019 and officially launched the brand in March 2025.
On Saturday, Lundgren shared a photo of himself that was taken at the fundraiser on Instagram.
"A big thank you to Novikov Beverly Hills and Hard Cut Vodka for a fantastic event supporting my good friend Arnold Schwarzenegger’s charity, After-School All-Stars.," he wrote in the caption.
The couple attended the All-Stars for Change charity event at Novikov Beverly Hills on Friday night. (Backgrid)

Lundgren and Schwarzenegger have been close friends and workout buddies for over 40 years. Shortly after they met, Stallone cast Lundgren as the iconic Soviet boxer Ivan Drago in 1985's "Rocky IV." Stallone served as Lundgren's mentor and trainer while he was training for his role in the hit sports drama.

title: Joanna Gaines reveals why she and Chip walked away from 'Fixer Upper' at the height of its success
summary: Joanna Gaines described a deep "soul weariness" that led her and Chip Gaines to walk away from "Fixer Upper" despite pressure to keep going.
story: HGTV stars Ben and Erin Napier shared their thoughts on the biggest challenges and rewards of working together as a married couple.
Joanna Gaines had success knocking on every door — and she decided to stop answering.
At the height of "Fixer Upper" fame, the home design and lifestyle expert and her husband, Chip Gaines, walked away from the nonstop grind despite pressure from their representatives to keep going.
Years later, Joanna explained that she had reached a point where she was experiencing what she called "soul weariness."
JOANNA GAINES KEEPS LIFE SIMPLE IN TEXAS AWAY FROM HOLLYWOOD SPOTLIGHT
Joanna Gaines details why she and Chip walked away from "Fixer Upper." (Christopher Willard / Disney)

"When you start realizing you're living on a thing that's now… the intentionality is gone, and you're just showing up… that doesn't feel fulfilling," she said on the "Joy 101 with Hoda Kotb" podcast. "It actually feels as though we're part of this machine that is like, 'What's the life here?'"

She added, "I would say that was our first pause of like, ‘We're doing all this and seeing great reward … this is wonderful,’ but also never at the expense of … our like livelihood, our happiness, our souls."
That pause would become a blueprint for how Joanna thinks about work — and burnout — today.

"Stopping in that moment was basically us saying … ‘What's worth it is, like are we healthy? Are we good? Is our family good?’ That's the most important thing. So that was really a very pivotal moment for us."
"Fixer Upper" turned Chip and Joanna into television stars, but even as the HGTV hit reached new heights, the couple knew they couldn't keep running at full speed forever.
Joanna Gaines said "Fixer Upper" fame left her with "soul weariness." (Getty Images)

The Gaines’s first stepped in front of television cameras when the "Fixer Upper" pilot aired in 2013. The series followed the husband-and-wife duo as they took on rundown homes in Waco, Texas, and transformed them into polished spaces for their clients — all while growing their increasingly influential Magnolia brand.
The show quickly became a hit, making Joanna and Chip familiar faces far beyond the world of home renovation.
COUNTRY STAR STEPS AWAY FROM MUSIC TO FOCUS ON HIMSELF AFTER FAME TOOK A TOLL
In September 2017, the couple announced they would end "Fixer Upper" after its fifth season, choosing to step away while the series was still riding high.
Joanna said she and Chip have spent almost 25 years building their business. But about three years ago, she said, they stopped seeing where they were headed.
"We stopped seeing vision. We stopped remembering, ‘Like why are we doing this?’"
The couple decided to take the summer off.
KATHIE LEE GIFFORD ADMITS SHE 'WANTED TO DIE' AFTER MISDIAGNOSIS AND MULTIPLE SURGERIES FOR CHRONIC PAIN
However, the decision wasn't consequence-free.
Joanna acknowledged that stepping away meant putting pressure on their team.
"Which meant disappointing our team, disappointing a lot of things … So it cost us something. It cost people something."
"But that three months was time for us to go, ‘We need a break. We need clarity. Why are we building this? What are we doing this for?’"
Joanna remembered the moment she felt the burnout was impossible to ignore.
Chip and Joanna shared how their son leaving for college changed their perspective on parenting. (Photo by Cindy Ord/Getty Images for SiriusXM)
"When you start dreading your days, like ‘I don't want to do that.’"
For Gaines, that sense of dread eventually became so pronounced that she found herself looking for almost any excuse to hit pause — even an unexpected illness.
"You start like wishing for a stomach bug or … 'Okay, maybe back surgery this year would be great.’ Like how do I force myself?" she laughed.
'80S POP STAR TIFFANY EMBRACES QUIET NASHVILLE ROUTINE AFTER LEAVING CALIFORNIA BEHIND FOR GOOD
Physical exhaustion, Joanna explained, is something she knows how to push through.
But the deeper exhaustion is different, she argued.
"So there's that part, but also just … where your soul just feels weary."
She described the "soul" as the deeper part of a person — the place that can run dry even when the body is still capable of performing.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
"From a physical standpoint, I can work till I can … I can push past the weariness the physical, but then you get to that layer of like the soul weariness and that's dangerous."
Joanna said that was the warning she is now determined not to ignore, describing the feeling as a "holy fear."
The couple, who created the Magnolia Market empire, has five children. (Nathan Congleton)
For the entrepreneur and television personality who built an empire by constantly creating, the hardest lesson may have been learning that she cannot simply outwork exhaustion.
The Magnolia Network stars tied the knot in 2003. Joanna and Chip are parents to five children — Ella, Drake, Crew, Emmie and Duke.

As the Gaines’s planted their roots in Waco, Texas, their Magnolia businesses took off.
The couple's Magnolia Market at the Silos in Waco pictured. (Getty Images)

After five seasons of "Fixer Upper," the original series ended in 2018. Magnolia Network programming later debuted on Discovery+ in 2021 before the linear Magnolia Network replaced DIY Network in January 2022.

title: Former Bond girl says next 007 should be 'another gorgeous man' as James Bond decision looms
summary: Alison Papworth weighed in on who should play James Bond in the iconic film franchise. The actress appeared in "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy."
story: Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.
The search for the next 007 is underway, and former Bond girl Alison Papworth has a clear message: Leave one thing untouched.

"What do I hope? I know they’re about to announce the next Bond, aren’t they?" the actress, who also works as a director for a London-based design and consultancy firm, told Fox News Digital. "And we’re all waiting with bated breath.

"If they’re true to the books, I hope it’s a man," she said. "A man, just a man. Yes, I think it would be very strange if it were a woman. Don’t you? It would be a totally different thing. So, I hope it’s another man, another gorgeous man."
AMAZON ANNOUNCES SEARCH FOR NEXT JAMES BOND IS UNDERWAY, AS HOLLYWOOD CASTING CHOICES COME UNDER SCRUTINY
Alison Papworth, right, was a Bond girl in "For Your Eyes Only" and "Octopussy," starring Roger Moore as 007. (Globe Photos/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)
Papworth’s comments came before Gary Oldman said on "The Morning Show" that his "Slow Horses" costar Jack Lowden could be the next James Bond.

"Jack, it’s been rumored that he’s on the shortlist," Oldman said on the Canadian talk show. "We’re going to find out pretty soon, aren’t we? Because they have picked him. They have made their choice, but they have not announced it yet. So, my fingers are crossed for Jack."

According to Deadline, Oldman later clarified his comments, saying, "There’s six people on a shortlist. I heard a rumor that they’ve picked James Bond, but they haven’t announced it yet, which is their prerogative. So, I do not know [who has got the part], but I’m hoping it’s Jack."
Jack Lowden attends the "Ella McCay" U.K. special screening at Picturehouse Central in London Nov. 24, 2025. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)
Amazon MGM Studios gained creative control of the James Bond franchise in 2025 after forming a joint venture with longtime Bond producers Michael G. Wilson and Barbara Broccoli.
WATCH: BOND GIRL ALISON PAPWORTH REVEALS HER HOPE FOR THE NEXT 007

In May, the studio announced the search for the next James Bond was underway. Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next installment, with Steven Knight writing the screenplay. Daniel Craig last played 007 in 2021's "No Time to Die."
People magazine reported that Paul Mescal, Jacob Elordi and Jack O'Connell are among the actors rumored to be in the running to take over the iconic role.

Producer Barbara Broccoli and producer Michael G. Wilson attend the world premiere of "No Time to Die" at the Royal Albert Hall in London, on Sept. 28, 2021. (Getty Images for EON Productions, Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer Studios, and Universal Pic)
The upcoming release will be the 26th Bond film in the more than 60-year-old franchise.
Daniel Craig was the last actor to play James Bond. (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)
Papworth appeared in 1981’s "For Your Eyes Only" and 1983’s "Octopussy," both of which starred Roger Moore.
"He was an absolute gentleman," she said. "Yes, I know everybody says it. I only have fabulous, fabulous memories of him being funny, telling the best jokes. Very dry, very droll.
Actor Roger Moore stands on the set of "Octopussy." (Corbis via Getty Images)

"One thing I really remember about him, when we were in India, there was a stuntman. I think it was a stuntman. He used to smuggle beef drippings in his luggage for Roger because he loved it. It was very funny, and it stuck in my mind all those years later."

Actor Roger Moore is seen here in London with seven of the women who appeared in "Octopussy." Back row, from left: Carolyn Seaward, Janine Andrews and Tina Robinson. Front row, from left: Joni Flynn, Alison Worth (who now goes by Papworth), Carole Ashby and Mary Stavin. (PA Images via Getty Images)

Being a Bond girl had its benefits. Papworth recalled being flown first class to Rio de Janeiro, where vodka was flowing for the cast, and she tried caviar for the first time. In between filming, she would observe Moore playing Backgammon at picture-worthy destinations.
But life on set wasn't always as luxurious.
Alison Papworth (seen here with her husband) is one of the few women who have appeared in more than one Bond film. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)

"It was the middle of winter doing the scenes for 'Octopussy' where we were fighting in the castle," Papworth recalled. "We learned to stunt fight, and it was supposed to be in India. But we were at Pinewood Studios, and it was below freezing. All the girls had these red bodysuits on with big capes. We were so cold, we had thermals on underneath. So, we probably looked about five pounds heavier."
Sir Roger Moore, who starred as James Bond, died May 23, 2017, at the age of 89. (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

Papworth didn’t expect to appear in two Bond films. She recalled a publicity director once telling her, "Once you’ve done a Bond movie, you get thrown on the Bond Girl scrap heap." But Broccoli, daughter of longtime Bond producer Albert "Cubby" Broccoli, had a different idea.
"You can imagine my surprise when I got the call from Barbara Broccoli saying, 'You’re on the next one, Alison,'" she said. "And it stayed with me. Bond has stayed with me. It’s changed my life.

"My two best friends, I met one on 'For Your Eyes Only,' Vanya Seager; she was another Bond girl. And I met my other best friend, Carole Ashby, on 'Octopussy.' Carol was there when my baby was born. Vanya and I, we speak every day. I speak to them both every day.
Alison Papworth, seen here with her husband, went on to become an interior designer. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)
"So, without Bond, I wouldn’t have those two incredible bonds."
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
Poster art for the 1983 James Bond film "Octopussy," directed by John Glen. (Alamy Stock Photo)
After appearing in two Bond movies, Papworth continued acting and modeling. By the time she reached her 30s, however, her modeling career was "leveling out."

"My husband had lots of properties, and I’d always loved interior design," she said. "I’m totally self-taught, but I’m passionate about it. And he just started giving me properties to do, and that developed into our business, which has been running successfully for all these years. I still love it. And after he died, I carried on. He taught me well."
Alison Papworth vacationed this summer with close friend Joan Collins, right. (Instagram.com/joancollinsdbe/)

Today, Papworth is a director at Camhall Design & Consultancy, an interior design company based in the U.K. It has completed projects in London, New York, Boston and the Bahamas. She also helped launch Lustre & Lustre London, which offers "luxury cleaning services."
Today, Alison Papworth heads Camhall Design & Consultancy, an interior design company based in the U.K. (Courtesy of Alison Papworth)

Papworth and her close pal, Joan Collins, also teamed up to raise funds for Shooting Star Children's Hospices. According to the organization's site, it supports, "babies, children and young people with life-limiting conditions, and their families, across south-west London, north-west London and Surrey."
Papworth still has fond memories of her time bringing the Bond stories to life.

Roger Moore meets the press with cast members from the James Bond film "Octopussy" June 1, 1983. (Getty Images)

"I love show business," she said. "I really do. It’s fabulous. And maybe I’m lucky that I’m not super famous, so I can have a private life. I’m not like my dear friend Joan who gets stopped everywhere. I’m lucky because I can dip in and out of it.

Ringo Starr hosts a charity fashion show in September 1986 featuring models Jilly Johnson, Cheryl Hart, Alison Worth, Carolyn Seaward, Camella and Carole Ashby. (Alamy)

"I still do signings," Papworth continued. "It went quiet through my 30s and 40s. And then, I don’t know. Bond fans are very good at tracking you down. I started to get invites to do signings. I remember doing my first signing in Birmingham at this huge exhibition center. My husband and my kids came because I was a first-time signer. There were all 'Star Wars,' 'Doctor Who,' astronauts, boxers and little me."

title: ‘Family Affair’ star Kathy Garver says failed remake ‘sucked,’ reveals what went wrong
summary: Kathy Garver called the 2002 "Family Affair" remake terrible, saying Gary Cole and Tim Curry couldn't replicate the original cast's deep warmth.
story: The ‘Family Affair’ star explains why the 2002 remake starring Tim Curry ‘sucked’ for ‘many reasons.’
Kathy Garver is not holding back about the failed 2002 remake of "Family Affair."

In a new interview with Fox News Digital, Garver — who is gearing up to celebrate the 60th anniversary of "Family Affair" by hosting a special marathon featured on Catchy Comedy — explained why the reboot lacked the chemistry, warmth and familial bond that made the classic show so beloved.
"Excuse my language, but it sucked," Garver, who portrayed Cissy in the original series, said. "And it did for many reasons."
'FAMILY AFFAIR' STAR TALKS 'SURVIVING CISSY,' SEEING ANISSA JONES FOR THE LAST TIME AND ALLEGED SITCOM CURSE
Kathy Garver, who played Cissy in the original "Family Affair" series, said the 2002 remake "sucked." (Everett Collection; Mark Gunter/Getty Images for ACCA Journal)
The original "Family Affair" premiered in 1966 and followed bachelor Bill Davis as he unexpectedly became the guardian of his late brother and sister-in-law's three children: Cissy, Buffy and Jody.
Brian Keith played Bill, while Sebastian Cabot portrayed the family’s butler, Mr. French.

The 2002 remake featured Gary Cole as Bill Davis and Tim Curry as Mr. French. Although Garver praised both actors, she said they brought entirely different qualities to the characters audiences had already grown attached to.
KELSEY GRAMMER ADMITS IT'S 'EXHAUSTING' WHEN MOVIES TRY TO ALTER HISTORY TO FIT MODERN TASTES
"I think it’s very difficult to do a remake," Garver said. "When they see Gary Cole, they say, ‘Well, that’s not Uncle Bill.’"
Cole was "great in ‘NCIS,’" Garver said, but "as you know, he’s no Brian Keith."
Keith’s appeal, she explained, came from the contrast between his tough exterior and his tenderness toward the children.
GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The cast of the television series "Family Affair" Aug. 10, 1966. Pictured from left are Anissa Jones as Buffy, Brian Keith as Bill Davis, Kathy Garver as Cissy, Sebastian Cabot as Mr. French and Johnny Whitaker as Jody. (Getty Images)
Brian Keith was "this macho guy, the ex-Marine," Garver said. "And here he is, this loving dad."
TIM CURRY'S CAUSE OF DEATH REVEALED
Garver also felt Curry’s portrayal of Mr. French was too far removed from Cabot’s understated performance.
"Tim Curry had a whole different take on it," she said. "It was very good, but it wasn’t in a situation-comedy vein. It was like the Tim Curry show.
"And, so, that didn’t quite mesh with Sebastian Cabot, who was a wonderful actor."
Garver described Curry’s Mr. French as "loud and boisterous," while Cabot’s version was "much more low-key."
Caitlin Wachs, Gary Cole and Tim Curry appear in the 2002 episode of "Family Affair," which aired Sept. 26, 2002. (Courtesy Everett Collection)
ORIGINAL 'LITTLE HOUSE' VILLAIN RETURNS FOR REBOOT WITH WARNING FOR NEW NELLIE
Cabot’s performance was also rooted in his character’s love for the children, Garver said, something she felt the remake failed to convey.
"He, too, did everything in love," she said. "And, basically, he loved the children. And I think that was missing from Tim Curry."
WATCH: ‘FAMILY AFFAIR’ STAR KATHY GARVER SAYS FAILED REMAKE ‘SUCKED,’ REVEALS WHAT WENT WRONG
The actress said the original cast members brought an authentic sense of family to the show because their characters genuinely cared for one another.
"Each individual person on the original ‘Family Affair’ had a family that they loved," Garver said.
‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS
Garver credited that emotional connection with helping the show stand out from other sitcoms of its era.
"I think it was a groundbreaker," she said. "It was the first of its kind — a single father, or a single uncle, single relative, that all of a sudden gets three orphan children."

The series also benefited from its production quality, according to Garver. She noted that "Family Affair" was among the early television sitcoms filmed in color and that many of the cast and crew members came from the movie industry.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS
The actress is gearing up to celebrate the beloved show's 60th anniversary by hosting a special marathon on Catchy Comedy.  (Getty Images)
"So, it was a real quality kind of show," she said.
Garver said the original series also featured "relatable characters" and storylines that continue to resonate with audiences.

"It has stories that endure today," she said. "And, so, it remains relatable, I believe, because it’s a family. And how — what do I do with the family? How do I deal with these problems? And it shows you that."
She also believed the warmth of the original series was reflected in the way the characters interacted with one another.
PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE
(L-R) Diane Brewster, Anissa Jones, Kathy Garver and Johnnie Whitaker in a scene from the TV series "Family Affair" in 1967. (Bettmann/Contributor)
"People really like each other — what a concept," Garver said. "People aren’t yelling and screaming at them. You have this very calm person that’s listening to you."
Garver said the original cast’s chemistry was also visible in their performances.
"Our creator, Ed Hartman, who was just a fabulous writer, creator and producer, told me, ‘Kathy, it’s in the eyes. You act through your eyes. What is coming through them?’
Garver said she would be opposed to a sequel.  (Getty Images)
"I think that warmth is something that’s sustained."
For Garver, the enduring appeal of "Family Affair" comes down to the emotional comfort it continues to provide viewers.
She described the show as "a comfort" and compared watching it to "taking a bite of the comfort cake."
"It’s not all this chaos, but something that’s beautiful and lovely and watchable," Garver said.

Catchy Comedy Network will celebrate the sitcom’s 60th anniversary with a special programming event Sunday, Sept. 13. Garver will host the marathon and share memories of portraying Cissy throughout all five seasons.

The event will feature eight of Garver’s favorite episodes, showcasing memorable storylines and Cissy’s journey from adolescence to young adulthood.

title: Mysterious disease sending young, healthy Texas workers into kidney failure
summary: A mysterious chronic kidney disease devastating Central America's agricultural workers appears to have surfaced among Texas laborers in extreme heat.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel joins 'America's Newsroom' to discuss the rise in chronic kidney disease happening across the world, how to avoid it,and how weight loss drugs could benefit those who have it.
A mysterious form of kidney disease that has devastated young to middle-aged agricultural workers in Central America and South Asia appears to have surfaced in Texas.

Known as chronic kidney disease of unknown etiology (CKDu) — or Mesoamerican nephropathy — the condition continues to baffle researchers, as some otherwise healthy adults develop kidney failure without having any of the traditional risk factors.

Chronic kidney disease can range from mild to severe, potentially causing fluid buildup and increasing the risk of high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and premature death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
CAN ALKALINE WATER ACTUALLY IMPROVE YOUR HEALTH? EXPERTS SEPARATE FACT FROM FICTION

But unlike typical cases, CKDu develops without common risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension and glomerulonephritis, a disease that inflames and damages the kidneys' filtering units, according to Dr. Gokul Paidi, a family medicine physician at Community Healthcare Network in New York.
"It typically strikes young to middle-aged adults, more often men, who work in agriculture and manual labor in hot, low-resource regions," he told Fox News Digital.
A mysterious form of kidney disease that has devastated young to middle-aged agricultural workers in Central America and South Asia appears to have surfaced in Texas. (Getty Images)
Several regional kidney diseases have been described over the decades, although not all are considered CKDu.

"Balkan endemic nephropathy has been documented since the 1950s, Itai itai disease in Japan was tied to cadmium contaminated rice, and Sri Lanka nephropathy has been studied since the 1990s," said Paidi, who has published a review on the condition.
Mesoamerican nephropathy – which was first described among sugarcane workers in El Salvador and Nicaragua in the late 1990s – is the form now being reported in the U.S., he noted.
"Disease often progresses rapidly over a few years, and dialysis and transplantation are rarely available."
Other locations have reported similar types of local epidemics, including Sri Lanka, India, rural Thailand and the Tierra Blanca area in Mexico, according to previous research.

"What’s emerging is that these are likely related conditions, essentially clusters of the same underlying disease process showing up in different farming and industrial regions around the world," Paidi said.
Unlike typical cases, CKDu develops without common risk factors such as diabetes, hypertension and glomerulonephritis, a disease that inflames and damages the kidneys' filtering units. (Getty Images)

Physicians at Houston safety-net hospitals, including Ben Taub, have treated otherwise healthy men in their 20s and 30s who presented with kidney failure — some with "Coca-Cola-colored urine," according to Texas Monthly.
They reportedly don’t have any of the typical risk factors that cause kidney disease, like high blood pressure or diabetes.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS
"What’s striking about the Texas cases is how closely they mirror what we saw originally in Central America," Paidi noted.

The patients are largely undocumented laborers from Mexico and Central America working in construction, roofing and outdoor trades in extreme heat – jobs where water breaks are often limited, he added.

Physicians at Houston safety-net hospitals, including Ben Taub, have treated otherwise healthy men in their 20s and 30s who presented with kidney failure — some with "Coca-Cola-colored urine," according to Texas Monthly. (Getty Images)

According to a review of Harris County hospital records cited by Texas Monthly, roughly one in six emergency dialysis cases in uninsured or undocumented patients had no identifiable cause, "which is consistent with CKDu," Paidi told Fox News Digital.

Some patients are reluctant to seek care or participate in research because of their immigration status, making it harder to track the disease in Texas and detect kidney damage before it becomes irreversible, experts say.
Common symptoms of CKDu
Experts refer to CKDu as a "silent disease" because most patients don’t initially complain of any symptoms.

Most patients – especially those who work in sugarcane fields – learn they have the condition during routine screening blood tests, according to Dr. Richard J. Johnson, a leading expert on kidney diseases and emeritus professor of medicine at the University of Colorado.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Later, it can cause typical signs of severe chronic kidney disease, including fatigue, sleep disturbances, nausea, weakness [and] shortness of breath from anemia," he told Fox News Digital.
By the time symptoms appear, and the disease is diagnosed, many patients are approaching end-stage kidney disease. (iStock)
By the time symptoms appear, and the disease is diagnosed, many patients are approaching end-stage kidney disease.
Many affected people are located in resource-poor regions where dialysis and transplants are often unaffordable or inaccessible, which can increase the odds of premature death, Paidi noted.
Potential causes
Heat stress is considered one of the leading suspected drivers of the disease, although its exact cause remains unknown, according to Johnson.

Experts believe a combination of occupational and environmental factors may gradually damage the kidneys. Strenuous outdoor labor can lead to repeated heat stress and dehydration, potentially compounded by exposure to crop pesticides and smoke from burning sugarcane.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Workers may also contend with potentially unsafe drinking water and rely on over-the-counter NSAIDs for pain — factors that, combined with repeated dehydration and heat stress, could further strain the kidneys, according to Texas Monthly.
Some experts suggest that improving hydration and shade, reducing work hours and starting earlier in the day could reduce kidney damage.
Diagnosis and treatment
There is no specific test for CKDu. Doctors diagnose it by ruling out other causes of chronic kidney disease, along with a patient's occupational and environmental exposures, Paidi said.
"Kidney biopsy is the closest thing to a gold standard, but isn’t practical for widespread screening," he added.
Heat stress is considered one of the leading suspected drivers of the disease, although its exact cause remains unknown. (iStock)

There is no disease-specific treatment for CKDu. Management focuses on controlling blood pressure, avoiding additional kidney injury — including from NSAIDs — and using dialysis or kidney transplantation in advanced disease, according to Paidi.
Some patients receive ACE inhibitors — medications commonly used to treat high blood pressure — but these drugs can sometimes worsen kidney function in people who are dehydrated, Johnson cautioned.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Disease often progresses rapidly over a few years, and dialysis and transplantation are rarely available, so mortality is high," he added – which highlights the importance of screening for the condition.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
For people living or working in agricultural or outdoor labor jobs, especially in hot climates, Paidi recommends getting kidney function checked with a primary care doctor at least twice a year.
"A simple blood test for creatinine (a waste product normally filtered from the blood by the kidneys) and a urine test for protein can catch early changes long before symptoms appear," he advised.

title: Common bedroom mistake could be quietly taking a toll on your health, experts say
summary: A Tulane University study links sleeping with light on to higher risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation, stroke and cardiovascular death.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a New Jersey-based nutritionist and author of "The Sleepdemic Solution," confirmed that household surroundings and ambient neighborhood conditions can directly interfere with restfulness.
A new study from Tulane University is raising fresh concerns about sleeping with a light on, linking nighttime light exposure to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease.

Researchers found that exposure to more than 3 lux of light — roughly the brightness of moonlight — was associated with increased risks of heart failure, atrial fibrillation (irregular and often very rapid heart rhythm), heart attack, stroke and cardiovascular death.
Experts spoke with Fox News Digital about the potential risks associated with sleeping with a nightlight.
THE DAYTIME HABIT THAT COULD TRANSFORM YOUR SLEEP, ACCORDING TO NEW STUDY

Sleep is partially controlled by the circadian rhythm, the brain’s internal 24-hour clock that regulates sleep and wakefulness, according to sleep expert and neuroscientist Chelsie Rohrscheib, Ph.D., a neuroscientist Neuroscientist and head sleep pesearcher at Wesper.
A new study from Tulane University is raising fresh concerns about sleeping with a light on, linking nighttime light exposure to a higher risk of cardiovascular disease. (iStock)

"The circadian rhythm is strongly influenced by light entering the eyes – light exposure signals the brain to suppress melatonin production, a hormone that helps regulate the timing of sleep, while low light levels signal the brain to produce more melatonin," the Michigan-based expert told Fox News Digital.
DIETITIAN REVEALS SIMPLE EATING STRATEGY FOR BETTER SLEEP — AND ONE HABIT TO AVOID

"As melatonin levels rise in the evening, they help prepare the brain and body for sleep. Light pollution from various sources in our bedroom can trick the brain into producing less melatonin, which can negatively impact sleep quality."
Health concerns
Consistent light exposure will chronically reduce overall sleep quality, Rohrscheib warned.

"Sleep plays an essential role in many biological processes, including body and brain restoration, hormone release, immune system functioning, cognitive processes such as memory consolidation, brain waste clearance and metabolic regulation," she said.
FINDING THE SLEEP 'SWEET SPOT' COULD HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, STUDY SUGGESTS

"When sleep is consistently poor, these processes do not function optimally, which in turn elevates the risk for many chronic health conditions such as hypertension, cardiovascular disease, stroke, type 2 diabetes, obesity, neurodegenerative diseases, certain cancers and mood disorders."
Consistent light exposure will chronically reduce overall sleep quality, an expert warned. (iStock)

A 2022 Northwestern Medicine study found that just one night of sleeping with moderate light exposure (100 lux) disrupted glucose regulation while increasing heart rate and sympathetic nervous system activity, as reflected by reduced heart rate variability (HRV), Rohrscheib noted.
MORE NAPS, HIGHER RISK? RESEARCH LINKS DAYTIME SLEEP TO HEALTH WARNINGS IN AGING ADULTS
Sleep impairment is also linked to increased risk of mortality, according to Ashley Curtis, PhD, sleep researcher and assistant professor at the University of South Florida College of Nursing.

"Emerging evidence even suggests that it affects the gut microbiome, everything from digestion to immunity," she told Fox News Digital. "While the immediate evidence is strongest for disrupted sleep health, the downstream risks to your long-term health are substantial."
For people with insomnia, who already experience chronic sleep disruption, bright light exposure before bedtime can make these underlying problems worse. (iStock)
Certain groups may be more sensitive to nighttime light than others, experts agree.

"Shift workers, children, older adults and individuals with insomnia or mood disorders are especially vulnerable to the effects of light on sleep depth," Alex Dimitriu, M.D., a double board-certified sleep medicine doctor and founder of Menlo Park Psychiatry & Sleep Medicine, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Curtis noted that older adults often become less sensitive to light, meaning bright or short-wavelength light has a weaker effect on suppressing melatonin than it does in younger adults.
"The caveat, however, is that older adults also experience a higher baseline prevalence of sleep disruption, which can bidirectionally impact the circadian system," she added.
"While blackout curtains are recommended for optimal sleep, you don't need to have absolute darkness to maintain a healthy sleep environment," one expert said. (iStock)
There is also some evidence showing that bright light has a more pronounced impact on melatonin suppression in men, the expert noted.

For people with insomnia, who already experience chronic sleep disruption, bright light exposure before bedtime can make these underlying problems worse, as it further interferes with the biological circadian rhythm, Curtis warned.
What type of light is the worst?
Blue wavelength light from TVs and phones is the most disruptive because people’s retinas are most sensitive to it, and it maximally suppresses melatonin, according to Dimitriu.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"Dim, warm, red-toned night lights cause far less circadian impact – these are natural sunset colors one would see in the evenings," he told Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Curtis agreed that warmer, dimmer light, which has a longer wavelength, doesn't have as much impact on melatonin production.

"Research shows that even if dim light impacts melatonin initially, it allows time for the body to recover," she said. "Therefore, it doesn't disrupt your sleep to the degree that brighter light does."
Practical changes to improve sleep
"While blackout curtains are recommended for optimal sleep, you don't need to have absolute darkness to maintain a healthy sleep environment," Curtis said.
"Dim, warm, red-toned night lights cause far less circadian impact."
The experts recommend implementing the following changes to cultivate a healthy sleep environment – even if it’s not pitch black.

title: Deadly bacteria detected as NYC orders emergency cleaning of cooling towers
summary: A health expert discusses why Legionnaires' disease outbreaks keep striking the South Bronx and other historically marginalized NYC areas.
story: Infectious diseases expert Dr. Tyler Evans explains the risks tied to Legionella found in Bronx cooling towers, which symptoms residents should watch for, and when exposure may require medical care.

Health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 rooftop cooling towers in the South Bronx after preliminary testing detected Legionella bacteria amid a growing Legionnaires’ disease cluster that has sickened nine people and left one dead.

The New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene issued orders to clean and disinfect the sites. Among the affected structures are cooling towers at major hubs, including Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital.
As public health workers work to clean the equipment, experts note that recurring outbreaks in these neighborhoods highlight deeper systemic vulnerabilities.
NYC LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK KILLS FOURTH VICTIM, 76 CASES REPORTED

"When we look at outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease, in New York City, we almost always see it in the Bronx or Harlem," Dr. Tyler Evans, CEO of the Wellness Equity Alliance and former first chief medical officer for New York City, told Fox News Digital.
"A lot of times, we see risk of infections taking place in historically marginalized communities."

New York City health officials ordered the immediate remediation of 10 South Bronx cooling towers — including units at Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital — after detecting Legionella DNA during a cluster investigation that has sickened nine people and caused one death. (New York Yankees/Getty Images)
The department identified the cluster following a surge in cases dating back to late August. Tests confirmed traces of Legionella in 10 of 24 sampled towers, according to city health officials.

PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests return results quickly, but cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria. Culture tests to confirm live bacteria can take up to two weeks, prompting city health officials to order immediate cleaning out of caution.

Late-summer weather has compounded the issue. High temperatures create ideal breeding grounds for bacteria inside industrial air-conditioning systems, which add water to the surrounding air, Evans noted.
HEART ATTACKS AND STROKES RISING WITH EXTREME WEATHER EVENTS, RESEARCH SUGGESTS
"Record-breaking temperatures lead to accelerating the risk of the bacteria basically cooking, getting out to become vaporized, and then producing exposure to other people," he said.

Legionnaires' disease, a severe form of pneumonia, cannot be spread between people, nor is it contracted by drinking tap water, the expert noted. Most healthy individuals are not sickened by exposure, but high-risk populations can face severe health consequences.

Preliminary PCR testing quickly confirmed bacterial DNA, but because it cannot distinguish between live and dead bacteria, officials mandated immediate cleanings while awaiting culture test results. (iStock)

"In terms of people ... to be concerned about, it's really older adults — typically 65 and older — or people living with comorbid conditions," Evans said, pointing to underlying factors like diabetes, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) or compromised immune systems.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Health officials urge anyone who has lived in, worked in or visited ZIP codes 10451 and 10456 since late August to monitor their health.
Key symptoms to watch for include high fevers, severe shortness of breath, chest pain and coughing up bloody mucus.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Evans noted that early medical care is crucial, as the illness responds well to standard antibiotic treatments when caught early.

"Infections fall into different buckets — bacteria, viruses, fungi, parasites," he said. "Bacteria are alive. Antibiotics are effective against bacteria because you can kill them, which makes it very treatable."

Legionnaires' disease is a non-contagious form of pneumonia spread through inhaled vapor — not drinking water — that poses the highest risk to adults over 65 and individuals with underlying conditions like diabetes or COPD. (iStock)
While city officials have taken quick action to inspect and clean the structures, Evans emphasized that long-term prevention requires sustained public investment.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Could we test all cooling towers across New York City on a regular basis during times of risk when it's hotter? Yes," Evans said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"City health officials do an amazing job, but it costs money. When federal funds are removed from public health, it's very hard to do more when you have less."
Fox News Digital reached out to Yankee Stadium and Lincoln Hospital requesting comment.

title: Woman loses best friend to ovarian cancer, then receives same devastating diagnosis months later
summary: A Minnesota woman diagnosed with stage 3B ovarian cancer after her best friend died from the same disease urges women to advocate for themselves.
story: Brian M. Slomovitz, MD, director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida, says ovarian cancer was once known as the "silent killer," meaning it was often undetected until it reached an advanced stage.
A Minnesota woman whose best friend died from ovarian cancer was stunned when she was diagnosed with the same disease less than a year later.

Becky Drexler was there to support her best friend, Connie Dahl, when she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in April 2015 at age 51. After a courageous battle, Dahl passed away in September 2017.
During her friend's cancer fight, Drexler began volunteering with the Minnesota Ovarian Cancer Alliance (MOCA).
CANCER SURVIVORS MAY SEE SURPRISING BENEFITS FROM ONE SPECIFIC EXERCISE, STUDY SAYS
After retiring in 2017, Drexler was making plans to travel, garden, volunteer and spend more time with family and friends – but those plans were interrupted by her own diagnosis in July 2018.
"I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer," Drexler, now 65, told Fox News Digital.
Becky Drexler (right) was there to support her best friend, Connie Dahl (far left), when she was diagnosed with stage 4 ovarian cancer in April 2015 at age 51.  (Becky Drexler)
Like her best friend, Drexler dismissed her own symptoms – including frequent urination, constipation, bloating and hip pain – as common signs of aging. She put off seeing a doctor at first.

"By early summer, I felt I was getting signs from Connie to nudge me along," she wrote in an essay sent to Fox News Digital. "Dragonflies represent Connie to me since she passed, and I saw them everywhere. I recall one afternoon being on my patio thinking, ‘Should I go see the doctor?’ when a couple dragonflies in my flower garden just wouldn’t leave me alone. I said out loud, ‘OK, Connie, I’ll go in and talk to the doctor.’"
ALCOHOL TIED TO SURPRISING CANCER DEATH PATTERN IN ADULTS UNDER 55, RESEARCHERS FIND
On Drexler's 57th birthday, her doctor called to say a CT scan had detected masses on both ovaries. After meeting with an oncologist, she had surgery four days later.
Drexler underwent six chemotherapy treatments (carboplatin and taxol) from September 2018 to January 2019.

"Those months were difficult but also filled with the support, love and laughter of family, friends, care team and MOCA," she said. "I knew Connie was part of my team as well – just in a different way."

After retiring in 2017, Drexler was making plans to travel, garden, volunteer and spend more time with family and friends – but those plans were interrupted by her own diagnosis in July 2018. (Becky Drexler)
Throughout Drexler’s cancer fight, she drew inspiration from her friend’s vow to "be positive, and to live, laugh and love to the fullest every day."

"This helped me greatly, as did attending MOCA support group meetings and talking to women who had or were experiencing the same things I was," she said. "There were times I wished Connie was still here so I could talk to her about what I was feeling physically and emotionally."
CURE FOR CERTAIN CANCERS IS ‘REALISTIC’ GOAL IN NEXT DECADE, PHARMA LEAD SAYS
In August 2020, Drexler’s cancer returned. She had surgery to remove the new tumor from her pelvic area.
"We discussed treatment options with my oncologist – she provided the pros and cons of standard chemotherapy, radiation, and no treatment, only monitoring," she shared.
"I was diagnosed with stage 3B high-grade serous ovarian cancer."

Ultimately, Drexler decided on targeted radiation, with chemotherapy as a backup option if radiation did not work or if there was another recurrence. After radiation was completed in January 2021, Drexler was again considered to have "no evidence of disease" (NED).
"I then began taking Lynparza, a PARP inhibitor maintenance treatment – something that was not even available for ovarian cancer patients when Connie was dealing with her cancer," she said.
From January 2021 until February 2026, while taking Lynparza, Drexler remained in NED status – "although there was always the concern in the back of my mind about when I would recur again."
VISION PROBLEM LEADS TO MAN'S STAGE 4 LUNG CANCER DIAGNOSIS, NEW DRUG EXTENDS SURVIVAL
In winter 2025, after experiencing gastric symptoms, Drexler underwent a PET scan. The scan revealed a tumor around her small intestine that had grown large enough to require surgery.

"Once the tumor was removed, it was confirmed to be a recurrence of my ovarian cancer," she said. "After recovering from surgery, I had another PET scan, which indicated a couple of spots were still present."
Becky Drexler (center) is pictured with other survivors presenting to medical students at Mayo Clinic in 2025. (Becky Drexler)
In May 2026, Drexler began an 18-week treatment cycle including carboplatin, taxol and avastin, which is expected to be completed at the end of September.
"I had a PET scan halfway through (late July), which indicated the treatment is working," she shared. "We were happy to learn that the spots were no longer visible and no new spots had appeared."
FDA APPROVES ONCE-DAILY PILL FOR DEADLY CANCER AFTER PATIENTS' SURVIVAL RATES NEARLY DOUBLE

Depending on the results of her next PET scan, Drexler said her next treatment will likely be an antibody drug conjugate (ADC) maintenance plan, a recently-approved targeted cancer therapy that has shown "exceptional results."
Throughout her cancer journey, Drexler has continued volunteering with MOCA, serving on its board of directors, participating on committees and reviewing grants for ovarian cancer research.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"It does make me think back to when Connie was dealing with her cancer and the treatments that were not available to her but are now available for me and other women," Drexler said.
"I believe I am still here because of the advancements in treatments. Developing a reliable early detection test for ovarian cancer remains one of the most critical research goals."
Symptoms to watch for

Ovarian cancer was once known as the "silent killer," meaning that women would get it and not know anything until the disease was in advanced, more aggressive stages, according to Brian M. Slomovitz, M.D., director of gynecologic oncology at Mount Sinai Medical Center in Miami Beach, Florida.
About 75% of women are diagnosed with stage 3 or stage 4 disease, according to the doctor.
Dahl, Drexler, Drexler's husband and Dahl's husband (left to right) are pictured at the Drexlers' wedding in 2002. (Becky Drexler)
In recent years, researchers have identified that ovarian cancer actually does have symptoms, noted Slomovitz, who is also deputy director of the Braman Comprehensive Cancer Center.
"The problem is they are sort of non-specific symptoms, things that could occur in everyday life – stomach pains, abdominal bloating, things like that."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"There may be an increase in abdominal girth, meaning patients complain that their pants are too tight or they're noticing something different in the way their body's shaped," the doctor said.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Those symptoms can also come with weight loss and decreased appetite, he noted: "They could oftentimes mimic gastroenteritis or eating a bad meal."
Any symptoms that persist or worsen over a period of one or two weeks should be checked out, the doctor advised.
‘Advocate for yourself’
To other women who may be experiencing worrisome symptoms, Drexler urges them to listen to their bodies.

"The early symptoms both Connie and I had were vague, like they are for most women," she said. "They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight."
"If something isn’t feeling right or a seemingly minor issue persists, and you think you might be concerned, see your doctor. Advocate for yourself."
"They seem like normal things that we can excuse away – we are aging, we are just stressed, we just need to eat better or lose weight."
For those who are diagnosed with ovarian cancer, Drexler emphasized that it’s important to see a gynecologic oncologist, as they have additional training in diagnosing and treating cancers.

Researchers have spent decades studying early detection and screening for ovarian cancer, Slomovitz said – "but unfortunately, no reliable method has been identified to diagnose women at an earlier stage."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

There is currently no recommended routine screening test for ovarian cancer in women at average risk, because available tests have not been shown to reliably detect the disease early enough to improve outcomes.
When ovarian cancer is detected at stage 1, the cure rate approaches 90%, Slomovitz said, underscoring the need for continued research into earlier detection.
