title: Pentagon reveals secret space weapons are already in orbit — but won't say what they do
summary: Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed the Space Force has on-orbit space control weapons, but the Pentagon won't say what they are or how they work.
story: CSIS space security expert Clayton Swope explains what the Space Force’s newly disclosed on-orbit weapons could be — and why they could give the U.S. an edge in a conflict.

The U.S. has weapons orbiting Earth that can be used to defend American forces from attacks in space, the Air Force secretary revealed this week in a rare public acknowledgment of capabilities the Pentagon has largely kept secret.

Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Monday that the Space Force now has "on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action," but declined to say what the weapons are, how they work or when they were deployed.

The carefully worded disclosure marks a shift in how openly the U.S. military talks about weapons in orbit as China and Russia develop their own capabilities to disrupt, disable or destroy satellites.
TRUMP TO TRANSFORM SPACEFLIGHT FROM SPECTACLE TO STATUS QUO TARGETING 3 LAUNCHES PER DAY
GPS satellite in Earth orbit. (Universal History Archive/Getty Images)

"Is there any question in the room, by anybody, about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?" Meink told reporters after his remarks at the Air & Space Forces Association’s Air, Space & Cyber Conference in National Harbor, Maryland — right outside of Washington, D.C.

"For over a decade, we’ve been talking about the fact, and we have expressed concern, that the Chinese and Russians were developing weapons for space," he continued. "We need to focus on making sure we can protect ourselves operating in that environment."
Exactly what the U.S. has put into orbit remains a mystery.

The U.S. has previously discussed placing weapons in space, including plans to deploy space-based interceptors capable of destroying incoming missiles as part of President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome missile defense system.

But Meink’s disclosure goes a step further: The Space Force already has weapons in orbit for "space control," a mission aimed at protecting U.S. access to space and, if necessary, denying an adversary the ability to use it.
The Pentagon has historically revealed little about the weapons developed for that mission, with publicly known U.S. counter-space capabilities largely based on the ground.
Troy Meink (Annabelle Gordon/Reuters)

"What the U.S. is going for is a wow factor here," Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, told Fox News Digital. "Wow. The U.S. has never talked about space weapons like this before."

"That's really what is exceptional and newsworthy about this revelation," Swope said. "The U.S. is saying we're putting weapons in space to make sure that our adversaries can't use space, or to make sure that we can continue to use space."

Meink appeared to make clear that the ambiguity surrounding the weapons is intentional. He told reporters his language was "very well thought out" and declined to say whether the systems are kinetic or non-kinetic. Kinetic weapons physically strike or destroy a target — think bombs, bullets and missile — while non-kinetic systems can disrupt or disable it without blowing it up — like cyber attacks or radio jams.

"There are a lot of factors that roll into how we talk about these things," Meink said, explaining that publicly revealing a capability can contribute to deterrence while disclosing too much about it can undermine that advantage.
"We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else," he said. That leaves a wide range of possibilities.
Fox News Digital did not hear back from the Space Force when reached for details of the weapon.
INSIDE AMERICA'S LASER REVOLUTION AS THE MILITARY NEARS BIG BATTLEFIELD BREAKTHROUGH

Swope said "space control weapons" could encompass everything from kinetic systems capable of firing missiles or projectiles at another satellite to jammers that interfere with satellite communications or lasers designed to temporarily overwhelm imaging sensors.

"We really don't have enough information to know precisely which one of these types of capabilities we're talking about," Swope said. "It's really anybody's guess what type of weapon we're talking about."
Golden Dome will need space-based radar capabilities. (Lockheed Martin)
FATAL AIR AMBULANCE CRASH EXPOSES GROWING GPS DANGER FACING US FLIGHTS
But whatever the Pentagon has deployed, putting a weapon in orbit rather than launching it from Earth could offer one potentially significant advantage: speed and surprise.

A weapon launched from Earth toward a satellite could potentially give an adversary warning that an attack was underway. A capability already positioned in orbit could dramatically shorten that window.
"Maybe something measured at dozens of minutes could be compressed into just mere minutes," Swope said.
"And you wouldn't have any indication that maybe a jammer was turned on, on the satellite, other than all of a sudden your signal is being interfered with," he added.

"If you can act fast without your adversary knowing, if you can have surprise, that gives you a strategic or an asymmetric advantage in combat," Swope said. "And having systems in orbit do just that."
Even observing the spacecraft itself may offer few clues about what it can do.
"Space is a very transparent place," Swope said, noting that governments and civilian observers can track where satellites are, how fast they are moving and what orbits they occupy.
"But what you'll see often is, oh, it's a satellite," he said. "It's a lot of technology with solar panels and antenna on it. And you don't really know much beyond that."
A satellite equipped to jam another spacecraft’s signals, for example, might look much like an ordinary communications satellite.
"Any signal can be a jamming signal," Swope said. "It just depends on if it's the one you want to receive, or the one that someone's trying to use to jam you."

The concept of weapons operating in orbit is not new. Swope pointed to the Soviet Union’s work on co-orbital anti-satellite weapons dating to the 1960s. Russia has continued developing counterspace capabilities, including systems designed to operate in orbit near other satellites.

China has also developed and tested technologies that could threaten spacecraft, including satellite-servicing and debris-removal systems that have legitimate civilian uses but could potentially be repurposed to interfere with another satellite.

President Donald Trump makes an announcement regarding the Golden Dome missile defense shield next to War Secretary Pete Hegseth in the Oval Office of the White House, May 20, 2025. (Reuters/Kevin Lamarque TPX Images of the Day)
Other forms of interference are already widespread.

"When we talk about jamming and spoofing and cyberattacks against space systems, these happen all the time, both from Russia and China and other countries like North Korea and Iran," Swope said. "There is so much jamming and spoofing happening around the world right now, it's almost ubiquitous."
Those attacks can target systems such as GPS and satellite communications without physically destroying a spacecraft.

That distinction could become critical during a conflict. Jamming, spoofing or cyberattacks may remain below the threshold that prompts a major military response, while physically destroying a satellite could represent a significant escalation.
"If you drop a bomb on a satellite ground station or you shoot a missile at a satellite in space, that's a big difference," Swope said. "That's a huge escalation."
The stakes are particularly high because modern U.S. warfare is deeply dependent on space-based systems for communications, navigation, intelligence, missile warning and targeting.
"Space is an enabler of joint operations," Swope said. "We can't do military operations the way that we do them today without satellites, without systems in space."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
China increasingly faces the same dependency, making control of space potentially decisive in a conflict between the two powers.
"Whoever has space and can deny that to their adversary has a huge asymmetric advantage in a conflict," Swope said.

"China depends on space as well, and their use of space for joint operations looks very much like the United States," he added. "Both countries, I would go so far as to say, depend on space to conduct military operations on Earth."

title: WATCH: 'Lifelong Democrat' admits she is ‘ashamed’ of party after son killed in illegal immigrant crash
summary: Democrat Elizabeth Carter told Congress she is "ashamed" of her party after her son was killed by an illegal immigrant truck driver in California.
story: Elizabeth Carter, who lost her son and daughter-in-law in an illegal immigrant-involved crash, said she is

Self-identified "lifelong Democrat" Elizabeth Carter (left) testified that she is "ashamed" of her party's handling of the immigration issue after her son, William Carter (center), and daughter-in-law, Jennifer Lower (right), were killed in a car crash involving an illegal immigrant semitruck driver. title: Trump-backed crypto bill fails to launch as Dems, Republicans unite to block it
summary: Sen. Cynthia Lummis declared the Clarity Act dead after Democrats and some Republicans blocked the massive crypto regulation bill in a key Senate vote.
story: Fox News chief congressional correspondent Chad Pergram reports on the Senate's upcoming test vote on landmark cryptocurrency legislation.
A colossal crypto regulatory package backed by President Donald Trump stumbled in the Senate, and another shot is unlikely.

The Clarity Act failed to move through a key procedural hurdle on Tuesday, serving proponents of the bill, including major players in the cryptocurrency industry and the White House, a major blow in their pursuit of folding the novel currency into the nation’s web of financial regulations.

Democrats dealt the bill a mortal blow, but a handful of Republicans with outstanding concerns, including Sens. Susan Collins, R-Maine, Josh Hawley, R-Mo., and Jerry Moran, R-Kan., were not assuaged, either. And with little time left on the Senate’s calendar and major bills piling up ahead of the midterm elections, the bill’s biggest backers believed that the Clarity Act might end up back on the shelf.
REPUBLICANS TARGET TRUMP'S CRYPTO EMPIRE WITH NEW PLAN, DEMS SAY IT FALLS SHORT
President Donald Trump during a meeting at Farmleigh House in Dublin on Sept. 12, 2026. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP)

"I think we're done. It's over," Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., the bill’s primary architect, said. "Because we've been working on this bill for over a year. And we've given them over 120 of their requests and that’s enough."
When asked if the bill would come back to the floor, Lummis said, "Nope."

A midnight hour update was made to the bill to try and pull anyone on the fence off to at least let the package move forward. But it wasn’t enough. And negotiations ran until the very end, just before the vote opened.
DEMOCRATS HAND TRUMP ONE POWER THEY SPENT YEARS FIGHTING

The issues with the package were many and varying among Democrats and Republicans. Several Senate Democrats were not satisfied with the ethics language baked into the Clarity Act that sought to slow the Trump family’s rapidly growing crypto empire.
That’s because Trump’s income between 2024 and 2025 erupted by about 250% — from just over $620 million to about $2.2 billion.

And much of that increase is attributed to his various holdings and ventures in crypto, which are run by his sons, Don Jr. and Eric, according to the president’s financial disclosure forms reviewed by Fox News Digital.
"We could talk a lot about it," Sen. Cory Booker, D-N.J., said of his vote against the bill. "But the simple thing is, it allows the corruption of the president to continue."

Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., who was working with Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., to strengthen the ethics provision in the package, told Fox News Digital, "We were actually getting very, very close, and at the last minute, the banking staffer from [Sen. Tim] Scott's office came in and just said, ‘negotiations are over.’"

"And so, I don't know what happened. You know, we were getting to the point where we were probably going to be able to pass, at least get the motion to proceed, move forward, and then, again, an ethics amendment vote," Gallego said.

"But I think they got scared with the fact that they had to take an ethics amendment vote. And that's why they killed it. They pulled it at that last minute, so it's bulls---. We were negotiating at the end. At the end of the day, they cared more about protecting the president's right to grift than trying to get a good bill on digital currency."
Others didn’t believe that the language dealing with foreign money laundering had enough teeth.

"I have not seen the kind of engagement yet from the Republican side when it comes to countering terrorist financing and cartel financing that would get me to a yes," Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., said. "I'm still engaged. I didn't get on board with the GENIUS Act till the very last vote."
TRUMP'S $5,000 DIVIDEND CHECKS WOULD COME WITH A MAJOR CATCH UNDER GOP SENATOR'S PLAN
Sen. Cynthia Lummis, R-Wyo., is the bill's primary architect. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
Still, some lawmakers argued they should at least move forward with the bill to tweak it as needed.

Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, was still undecided before the vote. He was worried about how bringing crypto into the fold could affect deposit yields at community banks and guardrails on the currency being "diverted for criminal purposes," but he argued the bill could be strengthened if they moved forward.

"What we used to do around here is something called legislate," Cornyn said. "You know where you'd actually vote to get on the bill, but then you amend it, and then you decide whether you're going to support it on the back end."

The bill’s failure does open up the Senate to speedily move to other legislative priorities, like Sen. Ted Cruz's, R-Texas, college sports bill to add protections to student-athletes and slow the big money train ripping through collegiate athletics.

"We committed to ensure that we got a vote on college sports," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said. "So we'll see if we have 60 [votes]. I don't know the answer for sure to that yet. I hope we do."

title: Kennedy Center board votes to immediately close main building over safety, financial concerns
summary: Fox News Digital confirmed Tuesday the Kennedy Center board voted to immediately close the building, citing safety and funding concerns.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

Fox News Digital confirmed Tuesday that the Kennedy Center board voted to immediately close the main building of the Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in Washington, D.C., citing safety and funding concerns.
President Donald Trump said shortly after the vote that the board agreed "almost unanimously" to close the building for safety reasons and begin the process of reconstruction.

Trump said the closure will take effect immediately, but renovation and reconstruction will not begin until the D.C. Circuit rules in the ongoing dispute over the board’s proposed use of his name at the Kennedy Center. He said Justice Department attorneys will seek an expedited appeal.
Trump also said $17 million he raised has been deposited into the Kennedy Center’s account "to keep it afloat."
KENNEDY CENTER CEILING PARTIALLY COLLAPSES AS TRUMP-LED BOARD PUSHES FOR 2-YEAR CLOSURE
The Kennedy Center board voted to close the main building Tuesday, citing safety and financial concerns. (Getty Images)
Two additional sources told Fox News the board approved the closure during a special meeting.

Earlier Tuesday, U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper blocked the board from putting Trump’s name on the building or renaming the grounds "President Donald J. Trump Plaza," ruling that such memorials require congressional approval.
Kennedy Center Vice President of Public Relations Roma Daravi said the board’s decision "reflects sound judgment and a clear prioritization of safety above all else."
EXCLUSIVE: KENNEDY CENTER BOARD MOVES TO NAME GROUNDS ‘PRESIDENT DONALD J TRUMP PLAZA'

"As the main building closes for urgent renovations — long overdue and desperately needed to protect the safety of patrons, artists and staff — the Center remains committed to pursuing a safe and efficient renovation through all legal means," Daravi said in a statement to Fox News Digital. "We intend to appeal today’s Court ruling and move forward with recognizing Chairman President Trump’s historic contributions to the revitalization of America’s Cultural Center."
The closure comes less than two weeks after part of the Kennedy Center ceiling collapsed during a rainstorm.
TRUMP'S NAME TO BE REMOVED FROM KENNEDY CENTER AS APPEALS COURT DENIES BOARD'S REQUEST FOR ADMINISTRATIVE STAY
Damage to the Kennedy Center ceiling after part of it fell into the main hall on Sept. 4, 2026.

Kennedy Center spokesperson Roma Daravi told Fox News Digital at the time that the structural failure demonstrated the "urgent need" for renovations and blamed "decades of neglect and deferred maintenance."
Trump said Tuesday morning that a security guard had passed through the area only shortly before the ceiling collapsed, and argued that the incident only demonstrated the building’s safety problems.
"A security guard had just passed the area, one minute prior to this ceiling collapse," President Trump said in his Truth post. "He was, therefore, 60 seconds away from certain death."
The Grand Foyer slab that fell roughly 60 feet during the recent structural failure weighed more than 150 pounds, according to information obtained by Fox News Digital.
KENNEDY CENTER DISPUTES ALLEGATIONS ON CONTRACTOR BIDS DESPITE DEMOCRAT SENATOR'S CLAIMS
A tarp covers the facade of the Kennedy Center in Washington, DC. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"The building is not currently built to last, the Chairman knows that because he is among the best builders in the world," said Brian Ballard, Kennedy Center Board of Trustees member. "We are lucky as a board and as an institution to have him at the helm during such a critical moment to save America's Cultural Center."
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
It was not immediately clear how long the Kennedy Center will remain closed or how Tuesday’s court ruling could affect the closure.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.
Fox News Digital's Brie Stimson contributed to this reporting.
Jasmine Baehr is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital, where she covers politics, the military, legal debates surrounding life and family policy, as well as faith and culture.

title: GOP Rep Thomas Massie introduces 8 articles of impeachment against War Secretary Pete Hegseth
summary: Rep. Thomas Massie read eight articles of impeachment against Pete Hegseth on the House floor, citing War Powers Resolution violations in Iran.
story: Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduces articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth on the House floor on Tuesday, Sept. 15, 2026.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced a resolution to impeach Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and read eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on the House floor Tuesday.

Massie formally entered a resolution to impeach Hegseth for "high crimes and misdemeanors" on the House floor for, among other things, allegedly violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973 in Iran and for his role in the operation that led to former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro's capture and extradition.

The first three of the eight articles of impeachment Massie introduced accused Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution of 1973, arguing that Hegseth's Department of War is "waging the Iran war despite no declaration of war, statutory authorization, attack on the United States, or imminent threat."

His first article seeks to establish "that the war was unlawful from its inception." The second article claims that Hegseth disobeyed Congress after both the House and the Senate directed the removal of troops from Iran. The third article claims that Hegseth is "continuing hostilities in Iran after expiration of the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day termination period and any potential 30-day withdrawal period."
4 HOUSE REPUBLICANS REBEL AGAINST TRUMP, VOTE WITH DEMS TO BLOCK IRAN WAR POWERS
U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduces a resolution to impeach War Secretary Pete Hegseth in connection with the U.S. conflict with Iran on Sept. 15, 2026. (House TV/Handout via REUTERS)

The fourth and fifth articles accuse Hegseth of refusing to minimize civilian casualties and engaging in extrajudicial killing, with the latter charge accusing Hegseth of "replacing maritime law enforcement with unauthorized lethal military targeting of suspected drug traffickers" during operations striking suspected narcotraffickers in the Caribbean Sea.
REP SETH MOULTON SAYS HEGSETH IS 'GUILTY' OF WAR CRIMES, LINKS HIM TO NAZIS TRIED DURING WORLD WAR II

Also related to military action in the Caribbean and South America, Massie's seventh article accuses Hegseth of the "Kidnapping of a Sovereign Foreign Leader" for his role in Operation Absolute Resolve, the January mission in which U.S. Special Forces apprehended and extracted former Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores from Caracas. Massie's article condemns Hegseth for doing so "without constitutional or legal authority."
War Secretary Pete Hegseth speaks during a press conference on U.S. military action in Iran at the Pentagon in Washington, D.C., on Mar. 2, 2026. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP/ via Getty Images)

Article six accuses Hegseth of using his authority to suppress the free speech of Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Ariz., by retaliating against the senator for his video in which the senator joined a group of other lawmakers in a video which critics claimed encourage active military members to disobey lawful orders.

The final article charges Hegseth with carrying out unlawful orders in Yemen. The article "charges Secretary Hegseth with initiating Operation Rough Rider without congressional authorization or an imminent threat to the United States, while also violating war powers reporting requirements. It further addresses extensive civilian deaths and unlawful strikes on civilian objects, rescuers, and other protected persons."
After reading out his articles for over an hour on the House floor, Massie closed out his introduction.
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., arrives for a House vote on the funding bill to reopen the government on Feb. 3, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

"In all of this, Secretary Hegseth abused the powers entrusted to him as Secretary of Defense by subordinating the constitutional limits on the use of military force and the laws governing the conduct of hostilities to his own policy objectives," Massie said.

Massie also added that Hegseth "has demonstrated that he will remain a threat to civilians, the lawful conduct of United States military operations, the integrity and credibility of the United States Armed Forces and the Constitution, if allowed to remain in office, and has acted in a manner grossly incompatible with his duties, and the rule of law.
This, Massie said, "warrants impeachment and trial, removal from office and disqualification to hold and enjoy any office of honor, trust or profit under the United States."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital contacted Massie's office and the Pentagon for further comment.

title: Kash Patel reveals FBI's capture of all 10 members of Most Wanted fugitive's list during hearing
summary: Kash Patel told the Senate Judiciary Committee the FBI captured a fugitive in Venezuela tied to Tren de Aragua, completing a historic clean sweep.
story: Kash Patel, testifying to the Senate Judiciary Committee, reveals that the FBI has caught all 10 of the FBI's 10 Most Wanted fugitives.

The FBI has apprehended all 10 members of the FBI's Most Wanted list during President Donald Trump's second term, FBI Director Kash Patel revealed during an appearance in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Tuesday.

Sen. Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, during his opening statements as the committee's chairman, lauded Patel and the FBI for their work in capturing nine of the 10 most wanted fugitives on the FBI's top 10 list.
Patel, during his opening remarks, corrected Grassley, revealing that his agency had just this past weekend caught the tenth fugitive.
"Mr. Chairman, I'm proud to announce today, and I hate to correct you, we haven't captured nine of the top 10 most [wanted] individuals on our list. We've captured 10," Patel said.
FBI CAPTURES TOP TEN MOST WANTED FUGITIVE WITH ALLEGED SINALOA CARTEL TIES, PATEL SAYS
FBI Director Kash Patel arrives to testify during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in the Hart Senate Office Building on Sept. 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"Just this past weekend, we captured a thug down in Venezuela who was on our most wanted list and on the run for years. He has been captured, apprehended and is on his way back to the United States of America. That's 10 of 10. Nobody in the FBI history has done that," Patel said.
HIGHEST-RANKING TREN DE ARAGUA MEMBER EVER EXTRADITED TO US SET TO APPEAR IN HOUSTON COURTROOM: DOJ
"We, the FBI, captured more than two and a half times the number of the top 10 most wanted fugitives on the FBI's list from the prior administration," he also said.

While Patel did not say the name of the fugitive during the hearing, the FBI earlier revealed exclusively to Fox News Digital that the 10th capture was that of Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre, the FBI's first ever "cyber fugitive."

Aguirre led "a large international conspiracy to steal millions of dollars from financial institutions in support of the Tren de Aragua, through an ATM jackpotting scheme since at least 2024," the FBI told Fox News Digital.
Anibal Alexander Canelon Aguirre's FBI 10 Most Wanted profile (FBI Media)

In addition to a clean sweep of the top 10 fugitives, Patel also revealed that his FBI has also captured six of the top 10 most wanted fraudsters on the top 10 fraudsters list, a compilation his FBI created during the current administration.
FBI TOUTS 6,000 ARRESTS, 44% HOMICIDE DROP ONE YEAR INTO TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN
Patel also outlined the broader progress the Trump administration has made towards making the U.S. safer.

"On top of that, we've captured six of the most wanted fraudsters around the world, taking the murder rate down 20 points is no easy effort. It requires a team lift, state, local and international partners. This includes results in cities like Baltimore, which reached its lowest mid-year homicide numbers in recorded history," he said.
TRUMP’S LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS, GUNS IN BLUE CITY
FBI Director Kash Patel is sworn in to testify during a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing in the Hart Senate Office Building on Sept. 15, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Win McNamee/Getty Images)

"This year in Memphis, we accomplished a 50% reduction in homicide for a city that had the highest per capita homicide rate in the country, thanks to the president's task force. And right here in Washington, D.C., we are on track to have the lowest homicide numbers since 1990," Patel added.
Fox News Digital contacted the FBI for further comment.
