WHO PAYS FOR US POWER BOOM? BLUE, RED STATES OFFER STARKLY DIFFERENT WAYS TO LOWER UTILITY BILLS AMID AI SURGE
An Ohio city is using floating solar panels on its drinking water reservoir to power its water treatment plant and cut millions in projected energy costs. (D3Energy)
Ohio puts 3,120 solar panels on a drinking water reservoir

Lima officially celebrated the completion of its Twin Lakes Floating Solar Project on Aug. 12. The final system includes 3,120 solar panels spread across about 3.6 acres of water, according to developer D3Energy. The 2-megawatt array sits on Lima's primary drinking water reservoir. That reservoir serves roughly 35,000 residents.

Next door, the city's water treatment plant processes about 14 million gallons of water each day. It also consumes more electricity than any other city facility. That makes the plant an obvious place to look for energy savings. Lima projects the floating solar system will save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over its lifetime. Earlier city estimates put first-year savings at roughly $200,000. For a city utility, that is serious money. Actual lifetime savings will depend on factors including future electricity prices and how the system performs over time.
How floating solar panels work
Instead of attaching panels to racks planted in the ground, engineers mount them on floating platforms. Anchors and mooring lines keep the array in position.

Lima uses Ciel & Terre's Hydrelio floating system. Its anchoring setup connects to the banks and reservoir bottom. The design also allows the array to move as water levels change. The project uses bifacial solar panels, which can capture light on both sides.

Electricity travels from the array to eight inverters onshore. From there, the electricity helps power the water treatment plant. The result looks a bit like a traditional solar farm that traded grass for water.
Why cities may want solar panels floating on water

Here is where the idea gets particularly interesting. Land costs money. It also competes with housing, businesses, agriculture and other development. Reservoirs already occupy space. Lima's floating array covers about four acres.

A land-based system producing the same amount of electricity would reportedly need at least 10 acres. That could make floating solar attractive to cities with limited open space. The panels can also sit near the facilities that need the electricity. In Lima, the water treatment plant sits right beside the reservoir. That reduces the need to find a distant solar site and then figure out how to move the electricity where the city needs it.

Researchers have also studied whether floating solar can help reduce evaporation by shading portions of the water surface. Of course, every reservoir comes with different conditions. Water depth, changing levels and recreational use can affect whether a project makes sense. Federal researchers also consider existing dam operations when evaluating potential sites.
LAWMAKERS TARGET ENERGY AFFORDABILITY THROUGH SWEEPING PERMITTING OVERHAUL IN NEW HOUSE BILL
Floating solar could help cities generate clean energy without using valuable land, but questions remain about long-term costs and water safety. (D3Energy)
What about putting solar panels on drinking water?

This was one of my first questions. These panels are floating on the same reservoir that provides drinking water to about 35,000 people. Lima's system uses Ciel & Terre Hydrelio floats made from high-density polyethylene, or HDPE.

Ciel & Terre says its floating system complies with the BS 6920:2000 standard for nonmetallic materials that come into contact with water intended for human consumption. Still, communities considering floating solar have more to evaluate than whether the structure can float safely.

The National Renewable Energy Laboratory has examined environmental and regulatory questions surrounding floating solar. Its research notes that projects can affect water bodies differently depending on the location. That means a system that works well on one reservoir may require a different design somewhere else.
The project cost millions before it could save millions

There is another number worth paying attention to. The Lima project cost about $5.3 million. Federal support played a substantial role in making the numbers work. The city received a $2.4 million Department of Energy grant. Combined with almost $900,000 in federal direct-pay tax credits, that support helped offset roughly half of the project's cost.

Those incentives covered a significant share of the upfront expense. That context is important when another city looks at Lima's projected $10 million in savings. A town considering floating solar would need to look at construction costs, financing and expected electricity production. Available incentives could change the calculation as well.

Lima began considering the project years before crews put panels on the water. City Council approved moving forward with the project in 2023. Construction began in 2025 before the system came online this August.
Could floating solar panels spread across America?

Lima may look unusual today, but floating solar has substantial room to grow. Ohio already has more than one project. D3Energy and ARP Solar completed a 1.5-megawatt floating array for Del-Co Water in Delaware, Ohio, in 2024. A 6-megawatt system in Monroeville is expected to come online before the end of 2026.

The bigger opportunity stretches far beyond Ohio. National Renewable Energy Laboratory researchers studied federally owned or regulated reservoirs across the U.S. They estimated those reservoirs have technical potential for 861 to 1,042 gigawatts of floating solar capacity.
That figure represents technical potential rather than a prediction that thousands of reservoirs will soon disappear under solar panels. Plenty of locations would never make sense.

Still, the scale helps explain why energy developers and local governments are taking a closer look at water. CyberGuy has covered this idea before on a much larger scale. India's Omkareshwar project showed how enormous floating solar installations can become. We have also seen developers rethink the shape of solar installations on land. One Texas company is building vertical solar towers designed to produce more power from a smaller footprint.
AMERICA’S BROKEN PERMITTING SYSTEM IS QUIETLY RAISING YOUR COST OF LIVING
Cities across the U.S. are exploring floating solar as a way to reduce utility costs while making use of existing reservoirs. (D3Energy)
Will floating solar panels lower your utility bill?

Here is the part I would keep an eye on. Lima expects to save nearly $10 million in electricity costs over the project's lifetime. But that does not mean residents will suddenly see a cheaper water bill. The city could use those savings in different ways. Lower energy costs could help cover other expenses, pay for infrastructure upgrades or ease pressure on future rate increases.

So, if a floating solar project comes to your town, there is one question worth asking: Will any of those savings eventually make their way back to you? That answer could determine how much this technology really helps the people paying the bills.
What this means to you

You probably do not spend much time thinking about how much electricity your local water plant consumes. Yet you ultimately help pay for that electricity through taxes, utility rates or both. Floating solar gives cities another way to attack that expense without buying a huge parcel of land.

It also raises questions you should ask before cheering on a project. How much will it cost? How much electricity will it realistically generate? What happens to the savings? You should also ask what testing and monitoring will protect the water supply. Those answers will tell you whether a floating solar project makes financial sense for your community.
Kurt's key takeaways

What I like about Lima's floating solar project is how practical the idea feels. The city already owns the reservoir, and its water treatment plant right next door uses a huge amount of electricity. So instead of finding another piece of land for solar panels, Lima put them on the water. Then there is the projected $10 million in savings. That certainly gets my attention. I want to see whether those savings hold up over time and, more importantly, whether residents eventually benefit from them. Lima also gives other cities something real to look at. We are seeing communities experiment with new ways to generate and store energy, from floating solar to massive battery projects. And who knows? The next solar project in your town may end up floating right on the water.

Would you be comfortable with thousands of solar panels floating on your town's drinking water reservoir if officials said the project could save millions, or would you need to see more long-term evidence first? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Amazon's Alexa for Shopping can now verify suspicious messages
summary: Amazon's Alexa for Shopping now lets customers verify suspicious emails, texts and phone calls against the company's own communication records.
story: Artificial intelligence is rapidly accelerating elder fraud schemes across the U.S., targeting older Americans who hold a significant share of household wealth. ScamSkeptic founder Matt Sanner joins 'America's Newsroom' to highlight how fraudsters utilize AI to mimic voices and create deepfakes. Sanner provides key strategies for families to identify these scams and protect their vulnerable loved ones.
We have seen plenty of scams borrow Amazon's name, and some of them look convincing enough to make almost anyone hesitate.

Earlier this summer, we showed you a fake Amazon email that claimed there was unusual activity on an account and pushed the recipient to "Sign In to Verify." The message even suggested a document might need to be uploaded. We have also warned about fake Amazon recruiting texts promising hundreds of dollars a day for easy remote work.
The stories change, but scammers keep coming back to Amazon because so many of us use it. A delivery warning or account alert can feel believable when you are already expecting a package.

Now Amazon is giving customers a new way to answer the question we keep asking when these messages arrive: Did Amazon actually send this? The company says about 360,000 customers contact Amazon customer service every year asking whether a message is real. Its latest answer is built into Alexa for Shopping.
AMAZON JOB SCAM TEXTS ARE SPREADING AGAIN WITH A NEW TWIST
Alexa for Shopping can now help U.S. customers check whether a suspicious text, email or call actually came from Amazon. (Amazon)
Here is how the new verification tool works, what it can tell you and why you should still keep your guard up when an Amazon message feels suspicious.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Amazon Alexa scam verification checks suspicious messages

Amazon says U.S. customers can now ask Alexa for Shopping whether an email, text, phone call or other message actually came from Amazon. Alexa for Shopping is Amazon's AI shopping assistant. It helps customers find products, compare items and manage shopping through natural conversation. Prime membership is not required to use Alexa for Shopping, but if you are considering joining, see our guide on how to get a cheap Amazon Prime membership at Cyberguy.com.

Now, you can also use Alexa for Shopping when something suspicious lands on your phone or computer. Instead of trying to judge a message by appearance alone, you can describe it to Alexa for Shopping.

You might ask: "Did Amazon send me a text about a delivery problem yesterday?" Or you could ask whether a Prime membership email came from Amazon. You can even provide details about a phone call from someone claiming to offer an Amazon refund. The verification tool then checks the information you provide against Amazon's own communication records.
How Alexa for Shopping checks an Amazon message

When you ask Alexa for Shopping about a suspicious communication, provide details about where it came from and when you received it. You can also tell the assistant what the message said. Amazon then compares those details with its records.
According to the company, its technology looks at information such as the sender and message content. It also considers timing and formatting.

That gives Amazon an advantage over tools that simply search for suspicious wording or potentially dangerous links. Amazon can compare the communication with messages generated through its own systems. The company says it only confirms a message as legitimate when the tool has complete confidence.
What Alexa tells you after checking a message

The answer depends on what Amazon finds. If Amazon can match the communication to its records, Alexa for Shopping tells you it came from Amazon. It can also provide details about the communication and account security advice.
If the message does not match Amazon's records, the tool tells you that the information provided does not appear to correspond with an official Amazon communication.
At that point, Amazon may advise you to check your orders directly in the app or contact Amazon through its official support channels. You should also avoid clicking links in the suspicious message.

There is another possibility. Alexa may tell you that it cannot verify the communication with certainty. If that happens, Amazon provides additional steps. You can submit more detailed information or use another Amazon verification option.
AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS
Alexa for Shopping now offers Amazon customers another way to check suspicious communications without relying solely on appearances. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
You can also forward a suspicious Amazon email

Alexa for Shopping is only one of Amazon's verification options. Earlier this year, Amazon launched verify@amazon.com. Anyone worldwide can forward a suspicious message to that email address and receive a response about whether Amazon sent it. You do not need an Amazon account or the Amazon app to use the service.

Amazon also offers a communication verification form through its customer service pages. So, if Alexa for Shopping cannot give you a firm answer, you still have another way to check before taking action.
Amazon reports suspicious communications you submit

There is another interesting part of the new feature. When you ask Alexa for Shopping to verify a communication, Amazon says it automatically reports that submission to its customer protection and enforcement team.

Those reports can help Amazon identify developing scam campaigns and bad actors impersonating the company. That means the suspicious text sitting on your phone could potentially help Amazon spot a larger scam targeting other customers.
Why fake Amazon messages keep fooling people

Amazon scams work because they often start with something completely believable. You ordered something last week, so a delivery problem sounds possible. You have a Prime membership, so an account warning gets your attention. Then the scammer adds pressure.

A fake email may claim your account has been locked. Another message might say someone placed an expensive order using your account. That urgency can push you toward a link before you have time to think.

We saw exactly that pattern in the fake Amazon account email we investigated. The message used Amazon branding and warned that the account had been placed on hold. The safest response remains simple. Do not use the link in the message to investigate the warning. Open Amazon yourself and check your account.
FBI HELPS TAKE DOWN AI PHISHING RING
Amazon is expanding its anti-scam efforts with a new Alexa verification tool designed to help customers identify fake emails, texts and calls. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
How to protect yourself from fake Amazon messages
Amazon's new verification feature gives you another way to check suspicious communications. However, scammers will keep changing their tactics, so these steps can help you stay safer.

Be cautious when a message pressures you to act immediately or threatens consequences if you do not respond. Scammers want you reacting quickly because slowing down gives you more time to spot something suspicious.
If a message claims your account will close or a package requires immediate action, avoid clicking its links. Check your Amazon account through the official app or website instead.

Watch for anyone claiming to represent Amazon who asks you to buy gift cards as payment. Amazon warns that it will never ask you to purchase a gift card to resolve an account problem or make a payment. If someone makes that request, stop communicating with them.

Be especially careful if a caller asks for sensitive account information. Amazon says it will never ask for your password or one-time passcode over the phone. If someone claiming to represent Amazon asks for those details, end the conversation and contact Amazon through an official channel.

Phone scams deserve extra caution because the number on your screen can look convincing. Scammers can spoof caller ID information and make a call appear to come from a familiar company. Seeing "Amazon" on your phone does not prove Amazon is actually calling. If someone unexpectedly calls about a refund or account problem, avoid giving them information. Hang up and check your Amazon account independently.

Phishing messages can expose you to malicious websites and dangerous downloads. That is why I recommend using strong antivirus software on your devices. Strong antivirus software can warn you about known phishing sites and suspicious links. It can also help detect malware if a scammer tricks you into downloading something dangerous. Of course, antivirus software cannot replace good judgment. Avoid clicking links in unexpected Amazon messages whenever possible. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com.

Amazon also points U.S. consumers toward the Better Business Bureau's Scam Tracker at bbb.org/scamtracker. Amazon has partnered with the BBB so consumers can search reports involving suspicious communications. You can search using details such as an email address or phone number. However, a lack of reports does not prove a message is safe. New scams can appear before anyone reports them. When in doubt, verify directly with Amazon.
Kurt's key takeaways

We have spent a lot of time showing you convincing Amazon scams because they keep arriving in inboxes and on phones. Scammers understand that Amazon feels familiar, which can make an urgent message easier to believe. That is why I think this verification feature has real potential. Instead of staring at an email wondering whether the logo looks right, you can ask Amazon whether the communication lines up with something it actually sent. Still, I would keep one habit above everything else: go around the message. Open Amazon yourself. Check your account from there. If something looks suspicious, use Amazon's official verification tools before you respond. The more ways we have to interrupt a scammer's sense of urgency, the harder it becomes for that scam to work.

Would you trust Alexa to tell you whether an Amazon message is real, or would you still want to verify it another way before taking action? Let us know your thoughts in the comments below. Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com.

title: Innocent woman says police use of Flock camera led to 13 days in jail
summary: Lindsey Brooke Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after a Flock camera flagged her Dodge Durango near a fatal Florida crash that killed three people.
story: Lindsey Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after license plate reader data wrongfully linking her to a crash that killed 3 people. Prosecutors dropped all charges after investigators identified another suspect. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Lindsey Brooke Isaacs was asleep at home when police arrived and told the 23-year-old that her car had been involved in a crash that killed three people. She knew they had the wrong person. Her black Dodge Durango showed no obvious collision damage, and she had a receipt showing where she had been.

Still, the investigation eventually led to her being arrested and 13 days in jail. "My heart was in my stomach," Lindsey told me on The CyberGuy Report Podcast at Cyberguy.com/podcast/. "I didn't know what was going on."

Months later, prosecutors dropped all eight felony charges against her and investigators arrested another woman in connection with the crash. Her case now raises a bigger question about how much weight investigators should give license plate camera data when a person's freedom is on the line.
Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.
Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com
LICENSE PLATE CAMERAS ARE TRACKING DRIVERS EVERYWHERE

Lindsey Isaacs says the ordeal left her shaken after she was arrested in connection with a deadly I-4 crash and later cleared of all charges. (Volusia County Division Of Corrections; The Law Offices of Patrick J. McGeehan, P.A.)
How a Flock camera became a major lead

The deadly crash happened on Oct. 4, 2025, along eastbound Interstate 4 near DeBary, Florida. Motorcyclist Joaquin Deno died. Flagler County Deputy Administrator Jorge Salinas and his wife, Nancy Salinas, also died. Witnesses reported that a Dodge Durango was involved.

Investigators found Lindsey's black Dodge Durango through a Flock automated license plate reader. The camera recorded her vehicle traveling eastbound near the Seminole and Volusia county line at 9:51 p.m. That camera was about three miles west of the crash scene. The crash happened around 9:53 p.m. That timing became especially important later.

Lindsey's attorney, Patrick McGeehan, said his team performed a time-distance analysis and concluded Lindsey was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. So the camera really did capture Lindsey's vehicle. The problem came from what investigators concluded from that sighting. Lindsey put it more bluntly during our conversation. "They just picked up my car off a camera and called it the end of the day. We got her."
Other evidence pointed toward a different Dodge Durango

The Flock camera hit was far from the only information investigators had. A 911 caller described a maroon Dodge Durango and provided part of its license plate number. Later, investigators also found red or maroon paint transfer on a Ford Focus involved in the crash.

Meanwhile, Lindsey drove a black Dodge Durango. A specialized Florida Highway Patrol team later inspected Lindsey's vehicle and reported finding no damage suggesting it had been involved in a collision with another vehicle.

That finding lined up with something Lindsey said she had been telling investigators from the beginning. "Where is the damage on the vehicle?" she recalled asking police. "Because I'm standing right in front of it and I don't see any damage." Still, authorities impounded her SUV. Months passed.
Lindsey Isaacs is arrested on charges seven months later

On April 17, 2026, Lindsey got a call from her attorney. She had to surrender that day. "They are arresting you for this crime," Lindsey recalled him telling her. She faced eight felony charges: three counts of vehicular homicide, three counts of leaving the scene of a crash involving death, leaving the scene involving serious bodily injury and reckless driving causing serious bodily injury. Lindsey spent 13 days in jail.

During our podcast conversation, she described spending her first several days in solitary confinement. She said she had a toilet, a sink and a metal sleeping slab covered by a thin mat. Her charges were so serious, she said, that jail officials initially kept her separated from other people.
Later, Lindsey was transferred to other sections of the jail. After her first bond hearing, she remained behind bars. "I was devastated, I was scared," she told me. "I thought my life was over."
HOW SURVEILLANCE TECH LED POLICE TO ACCUSE THE WRONG PERSON
Flock cameras helped identify a vehicle, but Lindsey Isaacs says investigators treated the camera hit as proof instead of a lead. (Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty Images)
A new investigation changes the case

The case finally began moving in a very different direction after prosecutors and a specialized Florida Highway Patrol team took another look. That team found no meaningful crash damage on Lindsey's Durango. Investigators revisited witness information and followed evidence pointing toward another vehicle.

On May 22, the State Attorney's Office formally declined to prosecute Lindsey on all eight charges. Authorities then arrested Alisa Lee Montalvo on charges connected to the crash. Prosecutors allege Montalvo was driving a maroon Dodge Durango. She faces nine charges, including three counts of vehicular homicide and tampering with physical evidence. She has not been convicted, and the charges remain allegations.

For Lindsey, the news brought enormous relief. "I felt like a new woman," she told me. "I felt free." Lindsey told me she later received an apology from the head of the Florida Highway Patrol. "It felt like a miracle," she said. "Another miracle from God that I was hearing it in person, face to face."

However, she also said the experience left lasting emotional and physical effects. "This took and is going to take maybe years to get better mentally, physically, emotionally," Lindsey said. Lindsey has since filed a federal civil rights lawsuit against two Florida Highway Patrol troopers involved in the investigation, alleging false arrest, wrongful imprisonment and malicious prosecution. Those claims have not been proven in court.
Flock Safety responds
We reached out to Flock Safety and the Florida Highway Patrol for comment. Flock Safety responded with the following statement:

"Flock cameras provide investigative leads; they do not identify perpetrators, determine guilt, or make arrest decisions. In fact, the complaint itself calls the Flock evidence 'exculpatory, not inculpatory,' meaning the evidence pointed away from Ms. Isaacs rather than implicating her: it accurately placed her vehicle three miles from the crash scene just two minutes before the crash. Characterizing her arrest as the result of Flock technology fundamentally misrepresents both the allegations and the role our technology played in this case."
The Florida Highway Patrol did not respond to our request for comment.
What a Flock camera can record

Flock cameras are automated license plate readers, often called ALPRs. They capture images of passing vehicles and use software to identify license plates. Flock systems can also capture vehicle characteristics including make, model and color. Each camera sighting can create a record linking a vehicle with a particular place and time.

For police, that can become an extremely useful investigative tool. A stolen car can appear on a camera. A vehicle connected to a missing person case could produce a lead. However, Lindsey's experience raises another question. What happens when investigators put too much confidence in one search result? We previously explored that concern after surveillance technology helped police accuse a Colorado woman of stealing a package. Her own phone location history eventually helped show where she had really been.
Lindsey blames how investigators used the Flock data

One of the most interesting moments in my conversation with Lindsey came when I asked whether she blamed the Flock technology or the way police interpreted its data. Her answer was clear. "I 100% think the second one you said, how police interpret the camera footage," she told me. That gets to the heart of this story.

The Flock camera captured Lindsey's vehicle traveling on I-4. The machine did what it was designed to do. Human judgment came next. Investigators had to decide what that sighting meant. They also had to weigh it against witness accounts, physical evidence and the condition of Lindsey's car.

According to Lindsey's federal complaint, the Flock hit three miles from the crash two minutes beforehand, ultimately helped her legal team argue that she was already beyond the crash location when the collision occurred. Technology can surface a lead. People still have to prove what that lead actually means.
FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES

Lindsey Isaacs spent 13 days in jail after investigators relied heavily on a license plate reader hit before charges were dropped. The case is fueling debate over how police use automated camera data. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)
Florida orders license plate readers off state highways

The debate over these cameras has now taken a major turn in Florida. On Aug. 31, the Florida Department of Transportation revoked permits for license plate reader systems within rights-of-way on Florida's state highway system.

FDOT cited the rapid growth of the systems along with reports of misuse and concerns involving data privacy and surveillance. Cameras covered by the order must be removed within 30 days. The agency also said it will stop issuing future permits for license plate readers within its jurisdiction.

However, that order does not eliminate every Flock camera in Florida. It applies to cameras within FDOT-controlled state highway rights of way. Local governments can take different approaches to cameras on city or county property. Several agencies have chosen to pull back further. Miami-Dade County, for example, announced that it would suspend its entire license plate reader program. Other Florida agencies plan to continue using cameras away from state highways.
Flock is adding new safeguards

Flock Safety has also announced significant changes to how its system operates. In August, the company announced that it was changing its recommended and default license plate data retention period from 30 days to seven days.
Flock also plans to require law enforcement customers to use its Audit Assistance tool by the end of 2026. The technology flags unusual search activity for review.

Case codes will also become mandatory for law enforcement searches by the end of the year. Flock says emergency searches can bypass that requirement, although those searches will be flagged for review. Those changes add oversight. Still, safeguards inside the software cannot determine whether an investigator has drawn the right conclusion from the information on the screen.
Your license plate can create a trail
Most of us probably drive past license plate readers without noticing them. A single plate scan may seem harmless. After all, anyone standing beside the road can see your license plate.
A searchable network changes the equation. Instead of someone seeing your vehicle once, a network of cameras can record when that vehicle passed particular locations.

We have already reported on Flock license plate cameras appearing at some Home Depot and Lowe's parking lots. We also reported on a Washington court ruling that found Flock license plate reader images can qualify as public records under that state's Public Records Act.

Lindsey told me she knew Flock cameras existed before her ordeal. She simply had no idea how much could ride on the information they collected. "I just thought it was like a traffic camera," she said. Today, her opinion has changed. "I feel very different about those cameras now."
POWERFUL CRIME-FIGHTING SURVEILLANCE GROWTH SPURS LAWMAKERS TO ISSUE WARNING: 'ORWELLIAN'
Lindsey Isaacs is suing two Florida Highway Patrol troopers after spending nearly two weeks behind bars in a case prosecutors later abandoned. (Volusia County Division Of Corrections)
What to do if police connect your vehicle to an investigation
If police tell you that your vehicle appeared in a license plate reader search tied to a serious crime, your own records could become important.

Save receipts and toll records that can help establish where you were. If your phone already stores location history, preserve that information too. Avoid changing or deleting anything related to the period investigators are asking about.

Doorbell cameras and security systems often overwrite older recordings. If footage could show your vehicle at home or somewhere else, preserve a copy as soon as possible. The same goes for dashcam video.

If authorities claim your car was involved in a collision, take detailed pictures and video showing its condition. Photograph and record each side of the vehicle and keep the original files with their date information intact.

A serious criminal accusation can escalate quickly. An attorney can help preserve evidence and communicate with investigators. Legal counsel can also examine whether the available data actually supports what police believe happened.
Kurt's key takeaways

I'm torn on Flock cameras. If somebody burglarizes my home, I want police to have technology that can help identify the vehicle that drove away. If investigators are trying to locate a missing person, a license plate reader could provide a valuable lead. But Lindsey's story shows what can happen when a lead begins driving the investigation instead of helping investigators test what really happened. Her black Dodge Durango had no crash damage. Other evidence pointed toward a maroon Durango. The timing of the Flock hit ultimately helped her attorney argue that she could not have caused the crash. Yet she still spent 13 days in jail. As I told Lindsey during our conversation, "I can't stand when technology is used in ways that it was never intended for." That is where I land on this. The technology can be incredibly useful. The people using it still need to challenge what they think they know before someone loses their freedom. Corie Walsh, the woman who obsessed over the Lindsay Clancy case and allegedly killed her 2-year-old son, sang a rendition of a Wizard of Oz classic while being questioned by investigators, according to reports.

Walsh, 40, who allegedly told officers she killed her son because she believed he was the "devil" and the "anti-Christ," belted out "Follow the Yellow Brick Road" from the movie classic, according to court documents obtained by The Sun.

title: AG Blanche unveils federal charges against 160 defendants in pandemic relief sweep

The Justice Department has charged dozens of people for suspected fraud related to the COVID-19 pandemic that resulted in hundreds of millions of dollars in losses, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Tuesday.

title: Seven noncitizens charged in North Texas election-integrity investigation
summary: The charges come as the Trump administration expands its election-integrity efforts.
story: Fox News correspondent Brooke Taylor gets an exclusive ride-along look with Homeland Security as agents ramp up arrests of immigrants who participated in voter fraud on 'The Story.'

Seven noncitizens have been charged in North Texas as part of a sweeping federal election-integrity operation, as the Trump administration ramps up its push to investigate and prosecute election-related crimes ahead of the midterms.

Fox News exclusively joined Homeland Security Investigations as federal agents carried out arrests in the Dallas–Fort Worth area, getting a firsthand look at how investigators are identifying and pursuing suspected cases of noncitizen voting.
U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of Texas, Ryan Raybould, announced that six defendants were indicted on Sept. 10, while a seventh was charged with a criminal complaint the following day.
Federal agents arrested six of the defendants over the following several days, while a seventh, who had been considered a fugitive, surrendered to federal authorities.
Voters cast ballots at a polling station during an election. (iStock)

"One of the individuals, an illegal alien from Mexico, actually was a 2023 convicted felon for lying on a passport application," Raybould said. "So this person has already interacted with our office, the Department of Justice, and chose to then again commit a serious federal violation."
In an exclusive one-on-one with Fox News, Raybould said the seven cases are only the beginning of his office’s efforts.
Earlier this month, the DOJ charged five people in Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Wisconsin in cases involving alleged illegal voting or fraudulent registration during the 2022 or 2024 elections.
"It’s important to clean up our elections and make sure that they’re free and fair," Raybould told Fox News.

"And my job as U.S. attorney is to prosecute cases and controversies. And so if fraud happens, whether it’s our elections, our health care fraud system, stealing from the American taxpayer, I’m going to go after it."
Raybould said prosecutors are focused on whether federal law was broken, not which candidate received an allegedly illegal vote.
FBI ARRESTS SUSPECT ACCUSED OF PAYING LA HOMELESS TO FORGE SIGNATURE USING REGISTERED VOTERS' IDENTITIES

"We don’t even know who they voted for, frankly, like we don’t care," Raybould said. "You can vote for whoever. That is not what we are focused on, it's the act. You're not allowed to vote if you're an illegal alien."
The federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters has drawn scrutiny from Democrats over how investigators are accessing and analyzing voter information.

Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, (D-N.Y.), and Sen. Alex Padilla, (D-Calif.), on Monday made public a complaint from an anonymous DHS whistleblower alleging that personnel working on the department’s "Unlawful Voter Initiative" were directed to access state voter records in ways that may violate state laws.
DHS has pushed back on those allegations.
The Department of Homeland Security seal displayed. (Getty Images)

"The Department accessed publicly available data from states’ voter rolls and cross-referenced them with known aliens in our systems. It’s not rocket science; it’s an easy step to secure our elections," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News.
Asked about the allegations, U.S. Attorney Ryan Raybould defended investigators’ use of federal databases and publicly available information.
"HSI has access to databases, and they have a right to access that database," Raybould told Fox News.
"They also can cross-reference that database with publicly available information."
Raybould compared the investigative approach to health care fraud cases, in which federal authorities analyze government data to identify potential outliers for further investigation.
WHITE HOUSE UNLOADS ON VIOLENT ‘CRIMINAL ALIEN’ NABBED AFTER INVESTIGATORS UNCOVER ELECTION OFFENSE
"We look at Medicaid data to identify outliers all the time, to pick targets," Raybould said. "Everybody should be in favor of making sure that illegals do not vote in our elections.
Raybould said prosecuting election fraud should have bipartisan support.

"If someone is illegal, and they vote in an election, that draws down the value of the vote of American citizens, and so it also undermines our democracy, and the vote is absolutely critical," Raybould said. "It's how we elect our leaders. It's an important voice for American citizens when they get to cast the ballot."

title: Lindsay Clancy judge indefinitely impounds juror names, citing safety and 'divisive' attention
summary: Judge William Sullivan sealed juror names in the Lindsay Clancy mistrial case, citing safety concerns and unauthorized identification of jurors.
story: Paula Devlin, one of 11 jurors on the Lindsay Clancy trial who believed she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her three children, explains the emotional toll of deliberations. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)
The judge in the Lindsay Clancy case has indefinitely sealed the jurors' names, citing safety concerns and what he called "significant and divisive attention" on the trial.

Judge William Sullivan issued the order on Monday and said while the court acknowledges that the jurors' names must be made available to the public, there is a "real and present" risk of harm to the jurors, stating he's impounding all names indefinitely until otherwise ordered.
Sullivan noted that there have been "identifications of jurors and their personal information without their permission" in explaining his reasoning for shielding the jurors' names.

"Some of the empaneled jurors have come forward and spoken to the media after the declaration of a mistrial on September 4, 2026. However, the majority of the jurors, deliberating and alternates, have maintained their anonymity, despite multiple requests to give statements," Sullivan wrote. "The Court concludes that there is a risk of immediate and irreparable injury should the list be made available to the public at this time."
LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR DENIES BIAS ALLEGATIONS, WANTS 'CONVERSATION STARTED' ABOUT WOMEN'S MENTAL HEALTH

In a separate filing on Monday, Sullivan ordered the impoundment of the clerk's list of potential jurors for the Plymouth County Courthouse for July 20 through July 24, during jury selection for the trial, "based upon threats and concerns over juror safety."

"Immediate and irreparable injury and dangers to jurors and to the administration, is real and present," he wrote, sealing the names of the entire jury pool for people who were called to jury duty during that timeframe.

title: Army veteran paratrooper who deployed to Iraq, Afghanistan before helping rescue Fox News reporter dead at 50
summary: Sean Michael Lee's cancer was linked to burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan, ending a life devoted to rescuing thousands from war zones and disasters.
story: Fox News senior correspondent Benjamin Hall and combat surgeon Dr. Joe Aldrete discuss their participation in the Tunnel to Towers 10th annual tower climb at One World Trade Center. Hall, who was critically wounded in Ukraine, emphasizes climbing to raise money for Gold Star families. Dr. Aldrete, who performed life-saving surgery, praises Hall's resilience, underscoring the importance of hope and community support for military families.
Sean Michael Lee, an Army paratrooper who helped evacuate thousands from conflict zones after his service — including Fox News' Benjamin Hall — died Sunday after a battle with esophageal cancer.
Lee was a 20-year veteran of the Army, having served multiple deployments to Iraq and Afghanistan as a member of the Army's storied 82nd Airborne Division, according to his obituary.

"He was, to his core, a paratrooper. Long after he took off the uniform, the values forged there remained the organizing principles of his life: duty, loyalty, competence under pressure, and an unwavering commitment to the person beside him," his obituary reads.
AMERICA’S PROMISE TO OUR AFGHAN ALLIES IS STILL UNFINISHED FIVE YEARS LATER
Sean Michael Lee in uniform. (Sarah Verardo/The Independence Fund)

Lee spent the years after his military service continuing to help people. In 2021, as Afghanistan's government was collapsing, Lee worked to help evacuate thousands during a chaotic withdrawal as a member of the nonprofit group Save Our Allies.

Just a year later, Lee was in Poland helping deliver supplies to the frontline in Ukraine in the midst of Russia's invasion. It was there that Lee became a key part of extracting Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall, who had been severely injured when Russian forces attacked his vehicle near Kyiv. Two members of Hall’s crew were killed in the attack.
BENJAMIN HALL TACKLES GRUELING ONE WORLD TRADE CENTER CLIMB ON PROSTHETIC LEGS TO HONOR FALLEN HEROES

"We got the call, we had just finished up a staff meeting with our folks back in the United States, and I can tell you that in about 90 minutes our guys were out the door and on the way," Lee explained to the Daily Caller during a 2022 interview.

Fox News correspondent Benjamin Hall visits "The Faulkner Focus" with host Harris Faulkner in New York City on March 15, 2023, to discuss his book, "Saved: A War Reporter’s Mission to Make It Home." (Roy Rochlin/Getty Images)
Lee also worked to help wounded veterans through The Independence Fund.

In 2024, Lee helped deliver life-saving supplies to survivors of Hurricane Helene in North Carolina. He lived out of a tent in the Tar Heel state as he helped deliver aid to communities where support systems had collapsed, according to his obituary.
LUKE COMBS AND ERIC CHURCH RAISE OVER $24.5 MILLION FOR HURRICANE VICTIMS AT STAR-STUDDED CONCERT FOR CAROLINA
Sean Michael Lee in front of a tent. (Sarah Verardo/The Independence Fund)
Most recently, Lee had been working under Secretary Doug Collins at the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs.

"Sean spent his life running toward the crisis. After more than two decades in uniform and multiple combat deployments, he continued that service through The Independence Fund, Save Our Allies and ultimately the Department of Veterans Affairs," Sarah Verardo, a founder of The Independence Fund and close friend of Lee's, told Fox News Digital.

"Whether evacuating Afghan combat interpreters and their families, helping establish field hospitals in Ukraine, or living out of his car to deliver aid in Western North Carolina, Sean went wherever he was needed most. His service knew no boundaries, and he never wanted fanfare or credit. He simply lived the ethos of ‘send me.'" Verardo said.
She also explained how Lee and her husband, a fellow member of the 82nd Airborne who was wounded in combat, forged a close personal bond.
Sean Michael Lee (C) pictured with Sarah Verardo. (Sarah Verardo)

"Sean walked alongside my husband for years following his catastrophic combat injuries and through his death, and for the better part of a decade, he was a constant presence in the lives of my three girls. He never missed a first day of school or a Halloween with us. Until his final breath, he remained that constant, living with us throughout his cancer battle and, even as his own world became smaller, still wanting to hear about dance recitals, science projects and all the ordinary details of their lives. He showed up for the defining moments and the ordinary ones because, to Sean, service was never a job or an assignment. It was simply who he was," she said.
"Sean was the definition of a quiet warrior. Our family has lost one of our own, and our nation has lost a patriot whose service never stopped," Verardo concluded.

He was part of the U.S. military's 2003 invasion of Iraq. He was also part of the storied Bravo Company in the 2-508 Parachute Infantry Regiment. Half of the company received Purple Hearts for an Afghanistan deployment that was documented in Ben Kesling’s book "Bravo Company: An Afghanistan Deployment and its Aftermath."
Lee's two best friends — Sgt. Michael Verardo and Sgt. Allen Thomas — both of whom deployed with him to Afghanistan, passed away before him.
Lee's cancer was the direct result of his exposure to the burn pits in Iraq and Afghanistan. He died at age 50.
VETERANS FACE SURPRISING THREAT AFTER CANCER DIAGNOSIS, STUDY REVEALS
Sean Michael Lee in Iraq. (U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) Defense Visual information Distribution Service (DVIDS))
"I can’t even begin to explain what the world has just lost," former MMA fighter and Special Forces sniper Tim Kennedy wrote in a post on Instagram.
"This country has lost one of the finest men ever to serve it," Kennedy's message continued.

"Sean redefined the word service. He did not just volunteer to put on the uniform and join the 82nd Airborne. He dedicated his entire life to other people. He put his life on the line more times than anyone can count. Wherever people needed help, you found Sean. Whenever I needed help, I found Sean," Kennedy wrote.
Sean Michael Lee of The Independence Fund pictured next to two men. (Sarah Verardo/The Independence Fund)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Lee's life "cannot be measured simply in years, deployments, jobs, or missions. It is measured in people who made it home because he went toward danger," his obituary, shared by Heritage Funeral & Cremation Services, says. "In wounded men carried to safety. In Afghan families given a chance to begin again. In communities that received help when they believed they had been forgotten. In veterans whose lives were better because he continued serving them after his own time in uniform ended. And in the children who simply knew him as Uncle Sean: the constant, fiercely protective man who showed up."

title: Pennsylvania man accused of plotting ISIS attack arrested with rifle and 190 rounds of ammunition: DOJ

A 21-year-old Pennsylvania man accused of plotting a violent attack on behalf of ISIS was arrested after FBI agents tracked him to a hotel and seized a semiautomatic rifle, five magazines and 190 rounds of ammunition, federal prosecutors announced Tuesday.

Jonathan Hunter Kramer, of Valencia, had allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS, offered to distribute explosives manuals online and said he was preparing for his "mission" but still needed a weapon before agents moved in, according to a federal criminal complaint.

Kramer is charged with receiving a firearm and ammunition, knowing or having reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony or federal crime of terrorism, including providing or attempting to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

The U.S. Department of Justice logo is seen on a podium before a news conference on May 4, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

The FBI had been aware since a 2023 investigation of Kramer, at the time a minor, when he was charged and adjudicated delinquent in Pennsylvania for his role in a plot to carry out a mass-casualty attack and for possessing child sexual abuse material, according to the Justice Department.

Authorities began investigating him again after an anonymous tip came in on March 19, shortly after his release from a juvenile detention facility. The tipster said Kramer was ordering "mysterious" packages and "talking to his friends from before" his juvenile adjudication.
FBI agents seized a semiautomatic rifle from Kramer's hotel room, authorities said. (Department of Justice)

Investigators said Kramer was using the online name "Hamza Al Rashid," claiming an affiliation with ISIS and offering to share explosives manuals. He allegedly wrote about preparing for his "mission" and said he was missing a "weapon."
On Friday, FBI agents watched Kramer leave his home with a bag and take a rideshare to a store, where he bought a disposable phone, according to the complaint.

Georgia police are searching for a man who police say was "infatuated" with a rubber duck in a stranger's hot tub.

The suspect is wanted for trespassing onto the homeowner's property and stealing their towels before fleeing the scene, according to the Chatham County Police Department, which said the man became "obsessed" with the rubber duck he found at the residence.

"He trespassed onto their property, used their hot tub, became obsessed with their rubber duck, then stole their pool towels. Police said that surveillance video from the home in the 9000 block of Whitefield Avenue shows the man trespassing between 2:15 a.m. and 5:30 a.m. on September 1.

Video footage shows the man swimming in the pool before hopping into the hot tub, where he became "infatuated" with a rubber duck and was seen "intensely interacting" with the toy, according to police.
"While in the hot tub, the man is caught on video becoming infatuated with a rubber duck. The video shows the man spending more than 10 minutes intensely interacting with the duck," police wrote.

title: Georgia mayor, 23, ousted 10 months after making history as state’s youngest mayor
summary: Jayden Williams, 23, was removed by the Stockbridge City Council after allegations involving public funds and communications with an 18-year-old student.
story: Jayden Williams faced intense questioning during an investigative hearing over his communications with an 18-year-old high school student. (City of Stockbridge Government)

Georgia's youngest elected mayor was removed from office just 10 months after taking the job following allegations that he misused city funds and exchanged sexually suggestive messages and images with an 18-year-old high school student.
Jayden Williams, who recently turned 23, was impeached by the Stockbridge City Council in the city south of Atlanta after taking office in January.
"The City of Stockbridge confirms that the City Council has taken formal action concerning the Office of Mayor," the city said in a statement on Sunday. "The Mayor has been removed from office."

Williams was accused of using his city purchasing card for more than $4,000 in personal expenses, including restaurant meals, clothing, haircuts and a movie, according to Fox 5 Atlanta. He reportedly spent $2,600 on gas and used a city vehicle for personal purposes.

Jayden L. Williams, 23, was removed from office on Sept. 12, 2026. (Paras Griffin/Getty Images)
The spending was reported after city workers noticed unusual transactions involving public funds and immediately notified management and the city’s legal team.

According to Williams’ testimony, he did not intend to use city funds and later repaid the money, Fox 5 reported. He further claimed the city-issued card looked similar to his personal card and said he later replaced the cards to avoid future confusion, the outlet reported.
FORMER DEMOCRATIC MAYOR OF STATE CAPITAL CITY PLEADS GUILTY FOR ROLE IN SIX-FIGURE REAL ESTATE BRIBERY SCHEME
Mayor Jayden Williams appears at a public investigative hearing on Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. (City of Stockbridge Government/Facebook)
Separately, Williams was accused of exchanging sexually suggestive messages and explicit images with an 18-year-old male high school student.

A police report noted that Williams did not commit any criminal violations because the student was considered an adult under Georgia law. However, police referred the matter for administrative review over potential policy and ethical concerns about an elected official's interactions with a student in what investigators described as a city-affiliated mentorship program, Fox 5 reported.

In a statement, Williams previously said he met the individual before taking office and that the student never participated in the city’s "Mayor for a Day" program, which Williams described as not a mentorship program.

story: Dramatic video shows a car engulfed in flames after a massive construction rig collapsed onto vehicles in Miami. (Credit: @CityofMiamiFire via X)

Four people were taken to the hospital Monday after a construction rig toppled onto three vehicles and a construction container in Miami, trapping two workers and igniting a vehicle fire, authorities said.
Miami Fire Rescue responded to the scene in the city's popular Brickell neighborhood near Southeast 12th Street and Brickell Bay Drive after the drilling rig collapsed at around 8 a.m.
"Miami Fire Rescue responded after a drilling rig fell onto three vehicles near SE 12 Street and Brickell Bay Drive," Miami Fire Rescue said in a post on X.
"The Technical Rescue Team units worked to safely free two trapped victims in a crushed container. Fortunately, the 4 patients transported were in stable condition."

Firefighters rescued two construction workers, ages 27 and 29, who were trapped inside the crushed construction container, Miami Fire Chief Robert Hevia said during a news conference.
Crews simultaneously extinguished a fire that erupted after the rig crushed a BMW, Hevia said.

"To be able to see the crane falling, pull the car in reverse and pop out of the back while the car’s on fire, really incredible," he said, describing how the BMW's driver managed to escape the burning vehicle.
The rig also crushed two unoccupied parked vehicles, he said.

"It was a very complex scene with a fire that was occurring, our crews were putting out the fire and our technical rescue team working simultaneously to cut through the Conex box, the construction box, and they were able to successfully extricate the two victims," Hevia said.
Earlier Monday, the Miami Police Department urged motorists to avoid the area.

"Due to a crane collapse, Brickell Bay Drive is currently closed between SE 12th Street and SE 13th Street. Motorists are encouraged to avoid the area, seek alternate routes, and expect delays. Please use caution and follow the direction of officers on scene," Miami Police wrote on X.

title: Lindsay Clancy juror says panel saw case as chance to 'make it better for other women'
summary: A Lindsay Clancy juror says the panel saw the case as a chance to help other women, a stance one trial attorney calls problematic for deliberations.
story: Criminal defense attorney David Yannetti discusses the aftermath of the Lindsay Clancy mistrial on ‘Sunday Night in America.’

One of the 11 jurors who wanted to find Massachusetts mom Lindsay Clancy not criminally responsible for killing her three children said the panel viewed the case as a chance to make things "better for other women" and families — a thought process that one legal analyst is calling "problematic."

"Even though we didn't know what was going on outside of our little bubble that we were in, we knew that this was a turning point, and this would be something that could change something to make it better for other women in the future, for other families," 65-year-old Clancy juror Paula Devlin told "CBS Saturday Morning" over the weekend. "You know, justice for those children is this never happening again."

According to Devlin, before the 11-1 deadlock that led to a mistrial, the jury had been split eight in favor of finding her not criminally responsible, two were undecided, and the holdout and one other juror were leaning toward a guilty verdict.
LONE HOLDOUT JUROR IN LINDSAY CLANCY TRIAL WAS ONLY BLACK PERSON ON THE JURY, PANELIST REVEALS: REPORT
Paula Devlin arrives home in Whitman, Massachusetts, Saturday, Sept. 12, 2026. Devlin was a juror in the murder trial of Lindsay Clancy. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

"Devlin’s statement is problematic," said Neama Rahmani, a Los Angeles-based trial attorney and legal analyst who has been following the case. "Jurors are supposed to decide cases solely based on the facts of that case. In the Clancy case, they were to decide whether she was criminally responsible."
The jury's role is to apply the law, not to make law, he said.

Several jurors and Clancy's defense attorney, Kevin Reddington, have claimed that the holdout at the end didn't show his fellow jurors the evidence that he believed pointed toward guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

LINDSAY CLANCY JUROR ADMITTED 'REASONABLE DOUBT' BUT STILL REFUSED INSANITY VERDICT, FOREPERSON SAYS
Lyndsay Clancy's defense lawyer, Kevin J. Reddington, arrives at Plymouth Superior Court, Plymouth, Mass., Sept. 3, 2026. (David McGlynn for Fox News Digital)

Separately, Clancy's husband Patrick Clancy vacationed in the Hamptons over the weekend, pictured with his new wife Rachel Danis at the Milk Pail farm stand on Montauk Highway in Water Mill, according to a photograph obtained by TMZ.

Patrick Clancy pictured shopping at the Milk Pail farm stand in Water Mill, New York, on Sunday, Sept. 13, 2026. Clancy is the former husband of Massachusetts mom Lindsay Clancy, whose trial on murder charges in the deaths of their three children ended with a hung jury. (TMZ.com)

title: Alaska teen rescued after 3 days in frigid waters reveals tragic end for 2 family members
summary: Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, clung to a capsized skiff for two days in the Bering Sea near St. Lawrence Island before a Coast Guard crew spotted him.
story: A 15-year-old boy was found kneeling atop an overturned skiff in Alaska’s frigid Bering Sea after clinging to the vessel for roughly two days — a remarkable survival ordeal that claimed the lives of his older brother and cousin. (Carlos Alexis Escartin via Reuters)

An Alaska teenager who survived nearly two days atop an overturned fishing skiff told his rescuers that his cousin had slipped away during the night and that his older brother remained beneath the vessel after the three were thrown into the frigid Bering Sea, according to rescuers and family members.

Derek Parker Aghnaanga, 15, was spotted Monday morning on the capsized skiff roughly four miles east of St. Lawrence Island after he, his 35-year-old brother Sidney Kulowiyi and their cousin disappeared during a fishing trip.

"Through the teeth chattering, he had mentioned that his brother was still under the skiff," Adam White, captain of the fishing vessel Northwest Explorer, told Anchorage affiliate KTUU-TV. "And then he said that, in the previous night, before our rescue, that his cousin had slipped away."
A GoFundMe page organized by relatives said Aghnaanga tried to hold onto his brother and cousin after they died, before their bodies were recovered.
TRAGEDY AT SEA LEAVES TEEN STRANDED ON OVERTURNED BOAT FOR NEARLY 3 DAYS IN FRIGID WATERS

This image taken from video provided by Carlos Alexis Escartin shows a teenager being rescued by a fishing vessel Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, in the Bering Sea near St. Lawrence Island, Alaska. (Carlos Alexis Escartin via AP)

A U.S. Coast Guard HC-130 Hercules aircrew from Air Station Kodiak spotted Aghnaanga atop the overturned vessel and dropped a survival raft and equipment before deploying flares to guide the Northwest Explorer to his location.
Crew members aboard the Northwest Explorer pulled Aghnaanga to safety and recovered the bodies of Kulowiyi and the teenager's cousin.
Aghnaanga was experiencing symptoms of hypothermia when he was rescued. Crew members wrapped him in blankets and used hot packs to warm him as the vessel transported him to Nome.

A 15-year-old survivor sits atop a capsized vessel while being towed to safety during a rescue operation off St. Lawrence Island, Alaska, Sept. 7, 2026, in this screen grab from a handout video obtained on Sept. 12, 2026. (Carlos Alexis Escartin/Handout via Reuters)

The three had departed the remote Alaska Native village of Savoonga on Friday for a fishing trip and planned to return early Sunday. Family members reported them missing Sunday night, prompting a search involving the Coast Guard, Alaska State Troopers and other state and local agencies.
MISSING 70-YEAR-OLD HIKER RESCUED AFTER DISAPPEARING FOR A WEEK IN REMOTE NATIONAL PARK

Colleen Walker, an aunt of the brothers, described Kulowiyi as a humble commercial fishing captain and provider for Savoonga, a village of roughly 800 residents where halibut fishing remains an important part of community life.

"We all cried and jumped for joy when the captain announced on the radio, 'We found a kid, he's alive, he's alive,'" Walker told The Associated Press, describing family members listening to the rescue effort.
The U.S. Coast Guard rescued a 15-year-old Alaska boy after he spent nearly three days in the frigid Bering Sea. A stock image of a boat in the Bering Sea is seen above. (iStock)
Kulowiyi left behind children, according to the family fundraiser, which had raised more than $42,000 toward a $45,000 goal as of Monday morning.

"Our hearts go out to the families, friends, and communities affected by the tragic loss of these two mariners," Rear Adm. Bob Little, commander of the Coast Guard Arctic District, said in a statement.
The Coast Guard Arctic District coordinated the search with the Alaska Rescue Coordination Center, the Alaska Air National Guard's 176th Wing, Alaska State Troopers and local authorities in Savoonga.
CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP
Neither the Coast Guard nor Alaska State Troopers have said what caused the skiff to capsize.
