Ukraine appears to agree with Schmidt’s assessment. The country’s new top general, Mykhailo Drapatyi, put innovation on a list of priorities he published after taking the position, saying Ukraine must learn faster than the enemy on the battlefield.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has also recently noted the jet-powered Shahed drones problem, saying the Defense Ministry and the military must work on capabilities to intercept them.
Schmidt expects artificial intelligence eventually to help computers direct drone swarms, using the results of attacks to improve how they fight.
“Humans can’t run a swarm of 1,000 drones, but a computer can,” he said. “So what I think will happen is computers will develop war plans within a swarm.”
For troops on either side, the drones already in use have made leaving cover dangerous.
“The battlefield today is a no man’s land where nothing moves because there are drones and anti-drones above you,” he said.

Small “first-person view,” or FPV, drones have become the war’s bullets, hunting exposed troops, Schmidt said. Russian aircraft also drop powerful glide bombs on Ukrainian positions, threatening soldiers who remain in their shelters.

Russian troops are suffering heavy losses, too. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry estimates that 42,020 were killed or wounded in August, roughly 1,350 a day, following 42,860 in July. It described August’s toll as among the highest since the full-scale invasion began.
Britain’s military chief, Air Chief Marshal Richard Knighton, said last week that Russia’s total casualties had reached 1.5 million, including approximately 500,000 dead.
“The death rate on the Russia side is horrible. It’s just horrible, and these are human beings, too,” Schmidt said.
Russia, meanwhile, has fitted some Iranian-designed Shahed attack drones with small, inexpensive Chinese jet engines, Schmidt said, making them faster than the interceptors Ukraine uses against them.
“So how do you intercept a faster drone? Well, you have to add your own jet engine to the anti-drone,” he said.

The jet-powered drones can reach a cruising speed of over 300 miles per hour, compared with a reported 110 miles per hour of older versions, according to the Open Source Munitions Portal, a weapons-tracking project.
Eight months ago, Ukrainian teams had been successfully countering Shaheds, he said. Now they are having to find ways to stop the faster versions.
He argued that Western countries should be doing more to learn from Ukraine’s experience and help it respond.
“How could we not be capturing this knowledge in the West to defend our own countries?” he asked.

Ukraine is also competing for American weapons. In March, Zelenskyy told NBC News he feared the war with Iran could divert U.S. supplies to the Middle East, although he said scheduled deliveries to Kyiv had not been disrupted at that point.

Schmidt warned the fighting could develop into “total war,” with Ukrainians determined to resist because they fear defeat would destroy their families. “Everything in both countries is a target for everything else. That’s just horrible,” he added.
He also held out the hope that powerful computer systems might deter both sides from attacking, each unable to predict how the other would respond.
“They need Western help,” he said of Ukraine. “In particular, they need some money, and they need technological help in order to counter this set of waves coming.”
“If that help comes, I think Ukraine can hold.”

title: 10-year Treasury yield tops 5% as oil surges and diesel hits all-time high
summary: Talks between Iran and Gulf countries about the future of the Strait of Hormuz were delayed after a key Saudi pipeline was hit.
story: The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield briefly topped 5% Monday for the first time since 2023 as the price of oil surged and the nationwide average cost of diesel fuel hit an all-time high.

Fears about those higher fuel prices feeding overall inflation are helping drive up yields. The Federal Reserve is widely expected to hike interest rates Wednesday for the first time since 2023. As of Monday, market odds for a hike were greater than 90%.

Longer-term bond yields, such as the 30-year Treasury bonds, rose to more than 5.37% on Monday, continuing to push to their highest levels since 2007. Consumer interest rates, such as those for mortgages, typically follow moves in bond yields.
Fuel prices shifted after Saudi Arabia shut a critical pipeline and talks about the future of the Strait of Hormuz were postponed.
The international oil benchmark, Brent crude, surged to more than $109 a barrel, while U.S. crude oil nearly hit $105.
By the end of the day, the increase had moderated. Brent closed the day up 1%, at $105.68 per barrel, and U.S. crude ended the trading session up 1.3%, at $101.39.

The East-West Pipeline, a key route for energy supplies, became even more critical because of the stalemate in the Strait of Hormuz, where vessel traffic has barely reached double digits in recent days.

U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said Monday that he did not have an exact time frame for when the pipeline may restart but that he was in contact with his Saudi counterpart and believed it would be “very soon.”

“I might have more of a time frame tomorrow,” he told Bloomberg Television. “They’ve been very carefully assessing what the damage was, what needs to be done, and I think more clarity on that will come out very soon.”

On Friday, the Saudi Energy Ministry said the pipeline was shut down “as a precautionary measure.” It did not say when the pipeline would be operational again. The attacks came as the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen made sweeping gains that tightened their grip on Bab el Mandeb, another critical waterway.
But the pipeline could be “out of service for weeks as the damage is repaired,” The Associated Press reported later Monday, citing two regional officials.

Adding to investors’ worries, a meeting between Iran and Persian Gulf countries about Hormuz was postponed Sunday afternoon. That meeting, set for Monday, was delayed “in the interests of consensus,” Oman’s foreign minister wrote on X.
Tehran said the meeting was postponed at the request of Riyadh.
On Monday, the Saudi state-run news agency said Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met with Adm. Brad Cooper, the commander of U.S. Central Command, in Jeddah.

Traffic through Hormuz remains at just a small fraction of pre-Iran war levels. On Sunday, just 14 vessels passed through the strait, and the numbers were only 12 Saturday, 11 Friday and nine Thursday, according to data from MarineTraffic.
With crude oil prices rising as a result of those disruptions, gasoline prices are, too. On Monday, the national average price of unleaded regular gas rose to $4.31 per gallon, according to AAA.
The national average price of regular gas has risen more than 45% since the U.S. and Israel launched the Iran war. The price of U.S. crude oil has soared more than 50% since the war started Feb. 28.
Since the start of the year, oil prices have risen more than 80%.
On top of that, the price of diesel fuel continues to set all-time highs. The national average price of diesel rose to $6.23 per gallon Monday, AAA also reported.
Diesel, which is used in everything from trucking to boat transportation to trains, has become a particular focus for economists who say it could cause almost everything to cost more.
“The cost of diesel gets into just about everything,” KPMG chief economist Diane Swonk said in a recent interview with NBC News.
“From running a farm ... [to the] cost of food, but also everything across the economy that’s shipped,” she said. When diesel prices rise, everything “gets that extra fee tacked onto it.”
Swonk predicted that the high cost of diesel will be an “inflationary problem” for months to come.
On Sunday, President Donald Trump sought to act on the issue by urging Ukraine to halt attacks on Russian energy targets.

Trump told reporters at the Irish Open in Doonbeg, Ireland, that he recently spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and asked him to stop targeting Russia’s oil refining infrastructure, particularly because of what is happening with the soaring price of diesel fuel.
“Mr. Zelenskyy has to do one thing,” Trump said. “He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia.”
“Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he’s causing a shortage of diesel fuel,” Trump continued. “Don’t hit diesel fuel, because that’s hurting the world.”

ING commodities analysts said Monday: “The growing scale and intensity of Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries this year have pushed Moscow to ban diesel exports. This has only tightened global markets, following Persian Gulf disruptions.”
Russia’s ban on diesel exports is set to expire at the end of September, but “clearly, there is the potential for further extensions,” ING’s team said.
After diesel prices fell as low as $4.77 per gallon in late June, new escalations between Ukraine and Russia have driven them 30% higher.
Since the start of the year, they have soared 75%.

title: China dismisses AI slowdown calls and blasts ‘fearmongering’ from U.S. tech leaders
summary: Urgent calls for a slowdown in the development of artificial intelligence may cite a grave threat to humanity, but China says the warnings are instead aimed at slowing its progress as America’s rival superpower.
story: HONG KONG — China has dismissed urgent calls to slow down the development of AI, rejecting the grave warnings as a bid to hobble the progress of America’s rival superpower rather than safeguard humanity’s future.
Beijing on Monday dismissed the intervention from U.S. tech leaders as “fearmongering” and part of a “Cold War playbook.”

It’s the latest sign that competition between the two countries could outweigh mounting safety concerns, after President Donald Trump also rebuffed the warnings from industry leaders and said his focus was on beating China on artificial intelligence.
The comments followed a lengthy essay published Saturday by Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and endorsed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and SpaceX founder Elon Musk.

Amodei said that companies should deliberately “slow the pace” at which they improve their models given the potential risks. He also said that a “Chinese lead in AI would pose grave danger for the United States and the world,” and called for the U.S. to restrict sales of key tech to China.
That message was not welcomed by Beijing.

“Fearmongering, confrontation and malicious competition will only disrupt the process of global AI governance and serve no one’s interests,” Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters at a regular news briefing Monday.

The state-run Global Times newspaper had a more blunt tone Sunday, blasting the call for an industrywide slowdown as “packed with containment provisions targeting China and is, in essence, a ‘Cold War playbook’ for the AI sector.”
AI has advanced at a breakneck speed, with models rapidly getting smarter, faster and cheaper. They have also frequently outpaced technical safeguards, fueling security fears.
Those fears have now reached a peak but also exposed just how far apart Beijing and Washington seem to be on cooperating to address them.
Amodei himself likened the situation to the Cold War arms race, telling CBS’ “‘Sunday Morning” that the two sides should work together but that he didn’t hold out much hope.
Altman similarly said on X late Sunday that “where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination.”
But that might not be compatible with Trump’s approach.

“We’re leading China in AI. We’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI wins,” the president told reporters Sunday. He criticized “very negative forces” for bringing up things “that won’t happen.”
While Trump rebuffs safety concerns, Beijing has acknowledged AI security risks.

State Security Minister Chen Yixin said Sunday that China must “accelerate the establishment of a system for preventing and controlling AI security risks.” Chen also said in the state-run China Cyberspace magazine that “we must engage extensively in international cooperation,” identifying AI as “a new track for strategic rivalry.”
The difference in approach on tackling AI progress is likely to be a central issue when Xi and Trump meet Sept. 24 in Washington.
Amodei’s essay came just a few days after U.S. agencies published an alert saying that top China AI companies have systematically copied cutting-edge AI models from American companies.
Beijing rejected this accusation that its companies had been “distilling” U.S. models.
China has also rejected any outside take on how its companies should pace development.

“They want to write the rules. I don’t think they want to follow anybody else’s,” Ja Ian Chong, an associate professor of political science at the National University of Singapore and a nonresident scholar at Carnegie China, told NBC News in a phone interview.
“There’s the sort of talk of cooperation, but the behavior suggests otherwise, and underlying that behavior, I think, is this deep mutual suspicion,” Chong said.

Chinese companies now offer advanced AI performance at a fraction of the cost of U.S. models, with President Xi Jinping pitching China as a pioneer of open-source models in contrast to those produced by most leading American companies.
At the BRICS summit in India on Sunday, he offered member nations help to develop open-source AI. Xi has also outlined a potential global governance framework on AI among the Global South.
How exactly could AI cause widespread danger?
Chong said the distillation clash highlighted the suspicion toward China in both the White House and Silicon Valley.

“It’s a bit like an arms race. And to get de-escalation there needs to be simultaneous neutral self-restraint and it’s difficult to see how that would come about in this kind of environment,” Chong said.
But not everyone is so pessimistic.

While a U.S.-China agreement on curbing AI progress may be a long shot, the countries could separately pursue greater regulation, said Theo Bertram, director of the London-based Social Market Foundation.
“The idea that we could see the domestic introduction of some safeguards in both countries is not impossible,” Bertram said in a phone interview.

“You do it domestically and it’s in everyone’s interest to learn and share and for there to be accountability,” he said. “Some greater accountability is one way of trying to mitigate what is inevitably going to be a growing political and public demand globally.”

title: Saudi shutdown of key pipeline limits oil flow as Yemen hits back against Houthis
summary: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, with the latest squeeze reverberating through the region Saturday as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.
story: Saudi Arabia has closed a critical oil pipeline after it was struck by drones launched from Iraq, with the latest squeeze reverberating through the region Saturday as attacks by Iran-backed Houthi rebels threatened to deepen the world’s energy crisis.

The 745-mile pipeline had helped Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest crude oil exporter, bypass the blocked Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass before the U.S. and Israel waged war on Iran in late February.

The Saudi Energy Ministry confirmed the shutdown of the East-West pipeline Friday, adding that drone attacks had resulted in a number of injuries and that its teams were “taking the necessary measures to secure the pipeline and assess its safety.”

Saudi Arabia said that, following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, it would not retaliate for now but reserves the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi Foreign Ministry statement.
The pipeline has been moving between 4% and 5% of global oil supplies, Reuters reported Friday.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq’s prime minister’s office. An umbrella group of Iran-backed militias in Iraq denied its involvement.
Iraq also closed two key border crossings with Iran, Iraq’s state-run news agency reported Saturday.

title: Strikes shut down key Saudi pipeline as Iran-backed Houthis tighten grip on crucial shipping lane
summary: Houthi rebels effectively completed a rapid push to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline on Friday, tightening their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes and delivering a dramatic boost to their backers in Iran.
story: Houthi rebels effectively completed a rapid push to take control of Yemen’s Red Sea coastline on Friday, tightening their grip on one of the world’s most important shipping routes and delivering a dramatic boost to their backers in Iran.
At the same time, strikes inside Saudi Arabia forced the shutdown of a critical oil pipeline, the country’s energy ministry confirmed Friday.

Saudi Arabia said drones launched from Iraq attacked its East-West pipeline, but said it would not retaliate for now following a request from Iraq’s prime minister, while reserving the right to take all necessary measures to protect its sovereignty, security and critical facilities, according to a Saudi foreign ministry statement.

An Iraqi military commander was dismissed early on Saturday after investigations confirmed the latest drone attacks targeting Saudi Arabia originated from Iraq, according to a statement by Iraq‘s prime minister’s office.

Houthi forces captured Perim, an island in the middle of the vital Bab el Mandeb Strait, several news agencies reported, citing multiple sources. A day earlier, the Houthis captured the historic port city of Mocha.

That was followed by an advance on the strategic coastal town of Dhubab and the apparent withdrawal of forces from the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized Yemeni government, from Perim, also known as Mayun.

The U.S. military is helping its Saudi counterparts to develop and coordinate targets inside Yemen, according to a U.S. official and a person familiar with the matter, after Saudi Arabia vowed a firm response to hostilities.

The Houthis and the opposing coalition have been fighting a civil war since 2014. The conflict has simmered for years but erupted into intense fighting again in recent weeks, raising concerns of a return to all-out war and posing a serious new threat to the global economy.

Effective Houthi control over Bab el Mandeb, a gateway to the Red Sea trade route that links Europe and Asia, could further imperil oil exports while granting Iran powerful new leverage in its war with the United States.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s biggest oil exporter, has had to rely on the Red Sea route given the disruption to the Strait of Hormuz, through which some 20% of the world’s oil used to pass, since the U.S. and Israel waged war on the Islamic Republic in late February.
If the Houthis are similarly able to threaten shipping along the Bab el Mandeb Strait, it could reduce oil supplies through another key waterway and deepen the world’s energy crisis.

title: Emma Bonino, leader of abortion and divorce battles that changed Italy, dies at 78
summary: Emma Bonino, who rose to political prominence as a leader of campaigns by the Radical Party that legalized abortion and divorce in the 1970s in heavily Roman Catholic Italy, against the objections of the Vatican, has died.
story: ROME — Emma Bonino, who rose to political prominence as a leader of campaigns by the Radical Party that legalized abortion and divorce in the 1970s in heavily Roman Catholic Italy against the objections of the Vatican, has died. She was 78.
Her party of recent years, +Europa, announced her death.

“Her life was a long struggle against everything that denies freedom: against clandestine abortion, world hunger, the stranglehold of party politics, female genital mutilation, punitive justice, genocide, and every form of authoritarianism,” the party said.

Italy’s conservative prime minister Giorgia Meloni paid tribute to Bonino, saying their different backgrounds and perspectives “never prevented me from acknowledging her significance and her role in our nation’s public life.”
“For decades, Emma Bonino has been a strong and recognizable voice in Italian politics, championing her ideas with determination,” Meloni wrote on social media.

Even after the Radicals’ political star faded, Bonino remained a key political figure and human rights campaigner active in Italy for over five decades. She served as a European commissioner for then-Premier Silvio Berlusconi and was a co-founder of the death penalty watchdog Hands Off Cain. But her bid in 1999 to become Italy’s first female president failed.

She remained known to younger generations as a sought-after political pundit, appearing frequently on Italian TV with her sharp wit and cutting insights. After her cancer diagnosis in 2015, she invariably appeared in public wearing colorful headscarves.
Bonino’s passing follows the recent death of several other feminist heroes, including activist Gloria Steinem and poet Robin Morgan.
Challenging the Vatican

Born on March 9, 1948, in Bra — not far from the northwestern Italian city of Turin, where carmaker Fiat’s factory drove the economy — she spent her childhood on a farm, where she was often tasked to pasture pigs, a lifestyle she described as “deadly boring” in a 2023 TV interview.
Bonino first got involved in Italian politics because she wanted to change the law. At 26, she became pregnant and had an abortion, even though it was illegal at that time.

Recalling the experience as one of the most humiliating of her life, in 1975 she was among the founders of the Information Center for Sterilization and Abortion, an organization that provided information and performed abortions before they were legalized.
The following year she was elected to the Italian parliament for the maverick Radical Party, a bastion of anticlericalism, civil libertarianism, feminism, liberalism and radicalism in Italy.
The party proposed itself as the strongest opposition to the Italian political establishment, seen as corrupt and conservative, and to the Catholic Church’s extensive influence on Italian society.

In 1978 abortion was legalized. That particular campaign may have been over, but Bonino had found her vocation: Politics was her life, and she became one of the most active leaders of the Radical Party and its successors.
She held key political roles in Italy and at the EU

A veteran legislator in Italian politics and an activist for various reform policies, she was elected six times as a Lower House lawmaker and two times as a senator. In 2017, she became the leader of +Europa, a liberal, European federalist party slate she launched ahead of the 2018 Italian general election.
An explosive presence in politics during her 50-year-long career, Bonino was one of the few Italian political figures who scored important achievements both at home and internationally.
Bonino won European exposure in a role she owed to then center-right Premier Berlusconi who, in 1995, offered her one of Italy’s two seats in the European Commission.

As a Commissioner she forged the EU’s consumer protection policy and created the European Commission Humanitarian Office, which is now the primary European humanitarian arm. It was this last portfolio, the humanitarian affairs, that she felt most strongly about.
She traveled to war zones — former Yugoslavia, Rwanda, Sudan, Afghanistan — and convinced Europe that humanitarian assistance couldn’t be an excuse for lack of political or military intervention.
In June 1999 she headed a slate named after her — Lista Bonino — at the European elections. It was an overwhelming success: The party got 8.5% of the votes and became Italy’s fourth political force.
Bonino served as foreign minister, trade minister and EU affairs minister in Italian center-left governments of the 2000s and 2010s.

She was one of the strongest advocates for a common European foreign and defense policy. “My passion is humanity,” she said in May 2025, when her hometown Bra granted her honorary citizenship. “I’ve got roots, I’ve got a homeland, a family, but precisely all that allows me to be a citizen of the world.”

She got involved with Arab women’s battle for equality in 2001 and started spending half her time in Cairo. She became fluent in Arabic — she had graduated in foreign languages at Milan’s Bocconi University — and built a network of intellectuals, politicians and prominent civil society figures.
She shared a humanitarian mission with Pope Francis

Never married, she maintained strong bonds with her family in Piedmont. “My father died before I could show him I could accomplish something,” she recalled in a 2020 interview with Vanity Fair. “He never understood my restlessness. He used to tell me: Emma, you are like Japanese poetry: beautiful, but I can’t understand it.”

In January 2015, she announced on Radio Radicale that she was suffering from lung cancer and was being treated with chemotherapy but didn’t plan to stop her political activity. In May of the same year, she said her cancer was in complete remission and eight years later appeared on a popular TV interview program announcing she was healed.
Over the years, Bonino cultivated a deep friendship with the late Pope Francis, despite their conflicting views on key ethical issues, including abortion and euthanasia.
In November 2024, Francis paid a home visit to Bonino — who had been just released from the hospital after treatment for respiratory problems — bringing her a bouquet of roses and chocolates.
A photo posted by Bonino on social media showed them both sitting in wheelchairs on her sun-drenched terrace in Rome.
Bonino said that during their conversations Francis always encouraged her to bring forward her humanitarian battles, defending those most in need.
When asked what battles she still needed to fight, Bonino used to say: “Many, too many. Human rights, world hunger, free scientific research ... Ten lives won’t be enough.”
Bonino is survived by her siblings, Domenica and Giovanni, and their children.

title: They led vigils for victims of Tiananmen. Now they’re facing time in prison for it.
summary: Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced Friday under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent.
story: HONG KONG — Three pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong who organized annual vigils for victims of China’s 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown were sentenced to prison terms between five and over seven years Friday after being convicted under a national security law that critics say has stifled dissent in the Chinese territory.

Lee Cheuk-yan was sentenced to seven years in prison, while Chow Hang-tung was sentenced to seven years and three months. Both had pleaded not guilty to charges of inciting subversion under the Beijing-imposed law.
A third defendant, Albert Ho, 74, was sentenced to five years and two months after pleading guilty, which can result in a shorter sentence.
Both Lee and Chow, who have been in custody continuously since they were charged five years ago, had pleaded for reduced sentences after the verdict. They had faced a maximum of 10 years in prison.

All three were leaders of the Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, which for three decades held annual candlelight vigils in honor of those who were killed on June 4, 1989, in a Chinese military crackdown on pro-democracy protesters in and around Beijing’s Tiananmen Square. The vigils, which drew tens of thousands of people a year, were the only large-scale public commemoration on Chinese soil of the Tiananmen crackdown, discussion of which is heavily censored in mainland China.
The alliance itself, which was also convicted, was fined 1.5 million Hong Kong dollars ($190,000) as part of the sentencing.

The trial, which began in January, was heard by three government-appointed judges who ruled last month that the alliance’s longtime call to “end one-party dictatorship” in China was an unlawful form of incitement to overthrow the country’s ruling Communist Party.

The United States, along with many other Western governments and United Nations human rights officials, condemned the Aug. 21 verdict as a further sign of Hong Kong’s deteriorating freedom of expression. The Tiananmen vigils “sought only to remember the past and honor the lives lost in that assault,” Assistant Secretary of State Riley Barnes said in a post on X.

During the trial, Lee, 69, a former lawmaker, told the court that the alliance was not calling to eliminate the Communist Party, but rather to allow the Chinese public to decide who governs them through free and fair elections.
The judges said the defendants were not being tried over their political views.
Chow, 41, a barrister who represented herself in court, said in her mitigation statement that the 206-page verdict “boils down to saying that pursuing democracy is a crime.”
“Believing that dictatorship is wrong and democracy is right — if that isn’t a belief, then what is?” she said.
Chow added that she had “no regrets” about her activism, saying she “would rather be a criminal than a person who betrays their conscience.”

Hong Kong, a former British colony, returned to Chinese rule in 1997 with the promise that its civil liberties would be preserved for at least 50 years. But residents of the once-freewheeling city have seen their freedoms significantly eroded since Beijing imposed a controversial 2020 national security law, which has also been used to jail other pro-democracy activists such as former media tycoon Jimmy Lai.

title: Flight carrying Zelenskyy to Norway was delayed in Moldova because of drone incursion
summary: Moldova had closed its airspace to protect planes flying over the country, delaying three departures, including Zelenskyy’s.
story: CHISINAU, Moldova — A flight scheduled to carry Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy from Moldova to Norway was delayed when authorities closed Moldova’s airspace because of a drone incursion, a government spokesperson said Wednesday.
Moldovan police said a Russian drone crashed on Tuesday in a sunflower field on the outskirts of a village in Riscani district, which caused four fires to break out but no injuries.

On Wednesday, government spokesperson Dumitru Ciorici said Moldova had closed its airspace on Tuesday afternoon to protect aircraft flying over the country at the time, delaying three departures, including the one carrying Zelenskyy.

Moldovan authorities confirmed the drone came down and exploded 100 miles from Chișinău International Airport. The airspace restrictions were lifted, and Zelenskyy’s plane took off later than scheduled.
The drone that entered Moldovan airspace on Tuesday crossed into neighboring Romania, a NATO member, where it was tracked through several northeastern counties.
The ministry said two F-18 aircraft of the Spanish Air and Space Forces were raised to track its trajectory before it re-entered Moldovan airspace.

On Wednesday, Moldova’s police said explosives experts discovered fragments of the drone that featured a propulsion system and characteristics similar to a Geran-type drone, which Moscow has used extensively in its full-scale war in Ukraine.

“Investigations identified the point of impact, where an explosion occurred and a crater of considerable size was formed,” police said, adding that specialists are continuing investigations “to determine the type and mass of the explosive payload.”
Ukraine neighbors both Romania and Moldova, and since Russia’s full invasion in 2022, both countries have reported dozens of drone incidents.

title: Oil surges past $101 to highest closing level since May as Iran conflict intensifies
summary: The price of oil breached the $100 threshold as new flare-ups between the U.S. and Iran stoked fresh concern for global energy markets.
story: The price of oil breached the $100 threshold Wednesday, as new flare-ups in the United States’ war with Iran stoked fresh concern for global energy markets.

Prices did not stop there and continued rising throughout the day. The international benchmark, Brent crude, jumped 3.3% to end the trading session at $101.21 per barrel. U.S. crude oil ended the day higher by 3.2% at $96.05 per barrel.
For both critical oil benchmarks, it’s their highest closing levels since May 22.

Wednesday’s spike came a day after the U.S. military said it destroyed five Iranian tankers in response to attempted missile attacks on a Navy warship. Tehran responded with attacks on U.S. ships and a base in Jordan, the latest bout of fighting in a conflict that remains unresolved after months of global economic disruption.
Elsewhere new attacks by a Tehran-backed rebel group set oil facilities ablaze in Saudi Arabia and threatened a significant new escalation in that conflict.
Since the start of the year, both oil benchmarks have risen by nearly 70%. Since the beginning of the Iran war on Feb. 28, both have risen by nearly 40%.
The price of oil appears to be of significant concern to the White House and Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, with consumers facing higher prices as a result.
On Wednesday, President Donald Trump said that he believes that gas prices would come “tumbling down” below $2 per gallon but not until “right after the election” this coming November.
“I think it’s going to take a little bit longer than the midterms,” he said.
Gas prices rose to $4.22 earlier Wednesday morning, the highest level since June 5.
Earlier in the week, commodities experts warned that oil prices as measured by Brent could rise to $120 or even as high as $150 per barrel if the stalemate with Iran continues to drag on.
Add to Google
Add to Google

Oil exports from the Middle East have dwindled since the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran in February. A fifth of the world’s oil supply had flowed through the Strait of Hormuz, the key waterway that has been throttled by Tehran in response.
While the U.S. military has managed to restore some shipping traffic through Hormuz, other key trade routes have also faced disruption.

Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen have attacked tankers in the Red Sea. This week, the group launched attacks on Saudi energy facilities that set oil sites ablaze and threatened a significant expansion of its conflict with the key U.S. ally.
Trump has shifted to a strategy of squeezing the Iranian economy with the U.S. maritime blockade, but recent days have seen a number of violent flare-ups.
